epub_9.title: The Sublime Somi Bridges African and Western Jazz
epub_9.text:
The Sublime Somi Bridges African and Western Jazz
Goings On
The Sublime Somi Bridges African and Western Jazz
Also: David Greenspan and Lupita Nyong’o onstage, the found-object art of Narcissister, a Hong Kong-born filmmaker’s exploration of family history, and more.
By Sheldon Pearce,Shauna Lyon,Dan Stahl,Marina Harss,Jillian Steinhauer,Richard Brody,Ryan Gellis
September 25, 2026
In the past two decades,
the singer Laura Kabasomi Kakoma, who performs music mononymously as
Somi
, has become a bridge between Western jazz and the jazz of Africa. An Illinois-born New Yorker of Rwandan and Ugandan descent who grew up in Zambia, she channels her diasporic upbringing into a synergized and singular sound—one anchored by a lovely, fluid voice that is paradoxically both calm and emphatic. She collaborated with the distinguished South African trumpeter Hugh Masekela, helped relaunch Sony’s Okeh Records as a jazz label, and released a tribute album for the singer-songwriter and activist Miriam Makeba. In 2021, Somi became the first African woman nominated in a jazz category at the Grammys.
Somi’s work is possessed by its duty to multiple traditions, something the singer has referred to as trying to “tell the truth” of her “dual inheritance.” Her songs have a stateliness to them, and yet they are unrestricted in their pursuit of a nuanced pan-African modality, the stories and rhythms at play therein. The 2014 album “The Lagos Music Salon” sought to embody the magic of the titular city, the result of an intracontinental cultural migration. Its 2017 follow-up, “Petite Afrique,” was even more ambitious: the song cycle deployed her sublime voice in search of answers for the African immigrants of Harlem as gentrification threatened the community they had built. Somi is also a playwright and actress; she wrote and starred in the Off Broadway musical “Dreaming Zenzile,” about Makeba, and starred, on Broadway, in “Jaja’s African Hair Braiding.” Her new album, “What Does It Take to Bloom?,” is a journey inward. Produced with Benjamin James, of the Nigerian highlife band the Cavemen, it is the most poised record of her career, and she brings its songs, and those of her many musical expeditions,
to Sony Hall, on Oct. 1
.—
Sheldon Pearce
About Town
Off Broadway
Marin Ireland’s semi-autobiographical play
“
Pre-Existing Condition
”
stars a vivid Lupita Nyong’o as A (the casting will rotate), whose world is reeling with confusion and shame following an incident in which her former boyfriend hit her so hard that she ended up on the floor. (She had tried to slap him a few days before, she offers wanly.) In impressionistic sketches, directed by Maria Dizzia, A struggles through sessions with a therapist (the appealingly forthright Dael Orlandersmith), group counselling (facilitated by the cheeky Sarah Steele and Orlandersmith), a date (Greg Keller, a nuanced charmer), her clueless mother (also Keller). She connects with a guy friend who respects her boundaries—after which, in a fraught meeting with her absentee father, A takes a step in a suddenly clear, positive direction.—
Shauna Lyon (Greenwich House Theatre; through Jan. 8.)
Off Off Broadway
Tom Stoppard’s
“The Invention of Love”
opens with the freshly dead classicist and poet A. E. Housman (a singsongy David Greenspan) reminiscing about his days at Oxford, astir with fin-de-siècle aestheticism and the titillations of his fellow-undergraduate Oscar Wilde (Sam Bolen, transfixing in this role and two others). But the young Housman (Yaron Lotan) took more interest in another student, the strapping Moses Jackson (José Espinosa), for whom his feelings were epitomized by the bond between Achilles and Patroclus, and between other close-knit comrades of antiquity, the field to which he devoted himself. Stoppard’s allusiveness is daunting but rewarding—something recognized by the director, Zachary Elkind, whose low-tech but resourceful staging refuses to pander.—
Dan Stahl (
Theaterlab
; through Oct. 3.)
Dance
The Gulf of Mexico may not be the first place one thinks of in relation to the ballet choreographers Frederick Ashton and Antony Tudor, and yet the excellent
Sarasota Ballet
has made itself a bastion of the twentieth-century British ballet repertoire. The troupe has also recently taken on several new dancers, including the princely Andrii Ishchuk, lately of American Ballet Theatre. On the program is Tudor’s moving portrait of repressed love and grim marital convention, “Lilac Garden”; the devilishly difficult balcony scene from Ashton’s “Romeo and Juliet,” with lots of tricky hopping on pointe; and the bucolic Peter Wright quartet “Summertide,” set to the shimmering second movement of Mendelssohn’s Second Piano Concerto.—
Marina Harss (
Joyce Theatre
; Sept. 29-Oct. 4.)
Pop
The chronically online pop-music fan is obsessive about positioning relative to the market—terms such as “flop era” and “Khia asylum” dominating their conversations about recognition and artistry—and few musicians have been more subject to this discourse than
Slayyyter
. A viral sensation in the halcyon days of Twitter, the singer was on the forefront of a sleaze-pop revival, and her self-titled 2019 mixtape, which found her at the intersection of the dance pop of the mid-two-thousands and the hyperpop still to come, put her on the shortlist of stars-to-be. When that call didn’t arrive, even Slayyyter questioned her career path, and she planned her March album, “Wor$t Girl in America,” as if it were her last, writing an ode to her iPod. Ironically, in doubling down on herself, she has never been more popular.—
Sheldon Pearce (
Terminal 5
; Oct. 3.
Brooklyn Paramount
; Oct. 4.)
Art
For nearly two decades, the artist
Narcissister
has developed a body of work marked by evocative visual motifs: an idealized feminine face mask, maneuvers involving contortion or sleight of hand, and nudity (her merkin is as common a sight as her mask). Her performances, which mischievously shred expectations of gender and race, have taken place in night clubs and at art museums—and on the TV show “America’s Got Talent.” For this exhibition, she constructed an installation out of found objects which doubles as a Rube Goldberg machine. Amid ropes, barrels, and exercise balls lies the show’s emotional core: seascapes painted by her uncle. She honors them, and a complex family legacy, in her indelibly risqué way, in a handful of performances, during which she wears her aunt’s dresses.—
Jillian Steinhauer (
Margot Samel
; through Oct. 10.)
Movies
In
“Palimpsest: The Story of a Name,”
the filmmaker Mary Stephen, a Hong Kong-born, ethnic-Chinese filmmaker, indeed explores the mystery of her own name. Her fascinating, playful quest involves the tangled background of her father, Henry Stephen. After his death, in 1986, she discovered a trove of his diaristic writings and home movies; with these archives she reconstructs his life and her childhood. The film unfolds his rough-and-tumble youth in Hong Kong; the turmoil of the Second World War; her father’s successful career in business; his encounter with the filmmaker’s mother, who called herself Hilda; and widespread divisions of class and race. The resulting stories involve surprising intersections of family and politics, of identity and imagination.—
Richard Brody (Streaming on OVID.tv.)
Bar Tab
Ryan Gellis discovers a beer counter in South Slope.
In sleepy South Slope, a local son in search of a beer bar walked past a familiar, long-shuttered laundromat. He did a double take—the rusting metal window grates were gone, the hulking coin-operated machines nowhere in sight, but an enticing sign had appeared on the awning: “BEER COUNTER.” Inside, people were still dealing in suds, albeit of a different kind.
Mash Inn
had transformed into an airy space, with a blond-wood bar and a forest of potted plants. Sixteen bronze taps stood ready to dispense craft ales, lagers, and a single cider. The patron chose a Cultivar: Cascade, from Wayward Lane Brewing, a hazy pale ale whose tiny bubbles effervesced so vigorously as to mist the upper lip. Two other townies were spotted, and their table was joined. These malt maestros, noting the surrounding mature crowd, wondered about the purported demise of drinking culture while they crunched through a bowl of puffed-rice snacks. The Mash Inn is a relative of the established brewski mecca Gold Star Beer Counter, in Prospect Heights, and has a similarly minimalist menu. In place of a liquor shelf (the establishment sells only beer and cider), there’s a turntable and a library of vinyl—this evening’s up-tempo jazz struggled to compete with the din of a full house. The next round was on the latecomer; a wild ale by the name of Arietta, from Fox Farm Brewery, floral and largely flat, had a pleasing barnyard funk. A Subglitch sour was rechristened “Jolly Rancher light.” It was conceded that the catalogue of brews outmatched the finite power of the liver. Upon decampment, the drowsy drinker is met with one final chance to imbibe, at the outside window, its sliding partition reminiscent of a Mister Softee’s. A growler of stout makes for pleasant company on the walk home.
P.S. Good stuff on the internet:
Designing the commonplace
How Leonard Cohen smell
ed
Victor Garber’s life-changing Jesus

epub_10.title: Ugly Baby Is Hot but Has a Personality, Too
epub_10.text:
Ugly Baby Is Hot but Has a Personality, Too
The Food Scene
Ugly Baby Is Hot but Has a Personality, Too
The beloved Brooklyn restaurant is back to serve a city in the thrall of Thai spiciness.
By Helen Rosner
September 20, 2026
If you listened carefully, almost two years ago, on the day that the Carroll Gardens Thai restaurant
Ugly Baby
announced that it would be closing, you could almost hear a wail of anguish rising up over Brooklyn. The chef, Sirichai Sreparplarn, a Bangkok native, opened Ugly Baby, in 2017, as a place to show off the fruits of years of gastronomic research into Thai cuisine: the fermented, spiced, herbaceous, sour, complex cuisine of the north; the turmeric-stained, shrimp-funked, chili-loaded cooking of the country’s south. Sreparplarn’s menu was expansive, but diners crammed into the narrow, color-saturated dining room for a few dishes especially, chief among them a duck
laab
and a
kua kling
(a beef dry curry), both obliteratingly spicy. The restaurant became known as not just one of the best Thai restaurants in town but the most reliable for nuclear detonation—the thinking person’s place to go get your face blasted off.
At the time, Sreparplarn said that he closed Ugly Baby because he just needed a break. The crowds had been relentless, the dining room packed and chaotic at all hours, and he wanted some time and space to regroup, and maybe to write a cookbook. He signed the lease for the space over to some former Ugly Baby employees who, with Sreparplan’s blessing, flipped it into Hungry Thirsty, a very good not-quite-tribute restaurant that specialized in Thai street food, and then he slipped off the stage. And now, almost as suddenly, he’s back: Ugly Baby is born again, in Williamsburg this time, in a window-lined, B.Q.E.-adjacent space more than twice the size of its former digs.
As before, Sreparplarn is in the kitchen, putting together dazzling dishes both familiar and unfamiliar; as before, Ugly Baby is a restaurant in which everything is amplified, not just the Scoville count. The room is again bright and brash, now with a long mirrored bar filling one wall, its bottles glittering in the maximalist space like a Marilyn Minter painting. The music is thumpy, up-tempo, and loud. While there’s more space between tables now—and a lower-level dining room for overspill—this is still not a restaurant built for quietude, or connection. You don’t come to Ugly Baby for conversation, any more than you would a night club; like a night club, it’s a place for (if you’re in the mood) pleasurable overwhelm, or (if you’re not—but then, why are you here?) unbearable sensory chaos.
Sreparplarn’s new menu is divided into three categories, in ascending order of smolder: the Laughs, for the soft-palated; the Cries, for the tenuously brave; and the Ugly, which I suppose is for the self-loathing, or the self-indulgent, or the asbestos-tongued. I think of myself as part of the last group—I’m no chili-head, seeking heat above all else, but I do like a little bit of that dopaminergic thrill, which the psychologist Paul Rozin, studying the human drive to burn ourselves with chilies, has described as “benign masochism.” So I dived right into the deep end, ordering without fear: a soft stir-fry of ground pork belly, umami-charged with shrimp paste and garnished with slivers of tomato-red hot peppers, whose heat crackled and blossomed against a caramel sweetness in the sauce. A salad of whole strawberries and bird’s-eye chilies, in a glaze-like dressing of sugar and fish sauce, was uncannily dessert-like—Would I like this on ice cream? I kept wondering—and yet certainly not a dessert, with all its thunderous layers of sourness and fishy-breathed complexity. I wished that I was in a quieter room when I took a bite of the
pad ped
, a dry curry of hanger steak and slippery tripe: it was rich and deep as nighttime, with a holy-basil brightness swaddled in some of the most violent heat I’ve ever experienced.
The new Ugly Baby was packed on each of my visits, with hopeful walk-ins circling the bar and clustered on the sidewalk outside. The staff, while friendly, seemed oddly unprepared for the crush. There seemed to be too few servers, too many hovering hosts urging diners into a quick turnaround, and far too many instances (one!) of forgotten, and sorely needed, additional bowls of heat-muffling white rice. It was clear, from the snippets of conversation that I could catch against the clamor of the sound system, that plenty of folks were having their first Ugly Baby experience, perhaps drawn by the challenge of its most ferocious dishes. But dining as heat-seeking can have a reductive effect. Just look at what happened to Jitlada, in L.A., which catapulted to international fame on the strength of a
kua kling
that the late critic Jonathan Gold declared “may be the spiciest food you can eat in Los Angeles.” Gold wrote that the rest of Jitlada’s menu was marvellous, too, full of dishes subtle and adventurous and spiky and soft, but the rest of his rave was mostly eclipsed by all the talk of spice.
Ugly Baby—both before and now—is more than just a place to show off your oh-so-manly pain tolerance, or to punish your digestive tract. One of my favorite dishes on the new menu (virtually none of which is carried over from Ugly Baby 1.0) is a soup, mild and gentle, in which bob wisps of omelette and soft pork meatballs, and you’d be remiss to breeze past a whole fried fish in the Laughs portion of the menu. A pompano on my visits, it was served with a tarry, sticky relish made up of seemingly every herb and spice and aromatic in the world, except for chilies. There were pumpkin fries, too, crispy and sweet, and a rich vegan curry of pineapple and eggplant thick with coconut milk, threaded with just a whisper of heat.
But we are, as a city, in the throes of a Thai-spiciness rapture. The owners of Hungry Thirsty expanded earlier this summer, with the opening of Hungry Spicy, in Chelsea; the new outpost is themed entirely around chilies and heat, almost to the point of goofiness, with chili-pepper décor and flame-shaped Mylar balloons floating against the fire-hued walls. I’ll admit that all the hype got to me: when I dropped in for dinner recently, I made sure that my purse was stocked with Tums and milky hard candies, to gird myself against flames of a strength I figured I’d never previously known. I shouldn’t have worried so much. The food was good, and plenty spicy—if not eyeball-melting, as one critic’s description of the
kua kling
as “genuinely unpleasant” had led me to expect—though most dishes felt a little single note, relying on the heat alone to bring the razzle-dazzle.
Helen, Help Me!
E-mail your questions
about dining, eating, and anything food-related, and Helen may respond in a future newsletter.
At Ugly Baby, even if half the room is there to performatively get their sinuses blown out, Sreparplan’s use of heat never feels like a gimmick. In a furnace-blasting
kang prik
(a dry red curry) of pork leg and pork rinds, the heat morphs from bite to swallow, blossoming from a distant crackle of fire to a sparking, tear-inducing electrocution. In the intervening seconds, there are other flavors dipping and twirling: the earthy sweetness of galangal and lemongrass, gently sulfuric garlic, vivid slashes of makrut lime. The heat deepens the dish; it doesn’t undermine, it doesn’t steal the spotlight. It ruins you, and opens you, and readies you for more. ♦
An earlier version of this article misidentified two of the dishes pictured.

epub_12.title: The President vs. the Press
epub_12.text:
The President vs. the Press
Comment
The President vs. the Press
Donald Trump’s behavior cannot be called unexpected at this point. What was noteworthy last week, however, was the way that the media responded.
By Jelani Cobb
September 27, 2026
Donald Trump’s decision, on September 18th, to summarily revoke White House access from three major news outlets—CNN,
Politico
, and MS NOW—is consistent with the mercurial, paranoid, and inscrutable style that has defined his political career but has been particularly prominent in his second term. Since Trump returned to the Presidency, his Administration has tended to justify its most belligerent actions by claiming national-security concerns or by couching said actions as an attempt to root out fraud. Earlier this year, the
Times
noted that Trump had cited “national security” as justification for acts as disparate as halting the development of wind farms off the East Coast, stripping union rights from federal employees, and continuing the construction of his behemoth ballroom. (He is now making the same argument regarding his colossal arch.) Accusations of fraud have been the reasoning for
doge
’s evisceration of the federal workforce,
ice
’s occupation of Minneapolis, and, just last week, the removal of three-quarters of a million people from the Affordable Care Act rolls. In a frenzied attempt to retrofit a rationale for Trump’s abrupt press ban, the White House turned to some version of both of these arguments.
Last Monday, the three news outlets filed suit, claiming that the ban violated their First Amendment rights. Dozens of other media organizations, including the
Times
and Condé Nast, which owns
The New Yorker
, filed an amicus brief in the case. Other outlets refused to participate in pool coverage of the President’s events, in solidarity with their banned peers. On Tuesday, the Department of Justice responded by claiming, in a brief, that the organizations had “threatened national security and spread falsehoods.” Further, it asserted that access to the White House is “a privilege,” not a right. Embarrassingly, the same day, the White House sent
Politico
a letter citing its reporting on the Iran war, which noted the concerns of an anonymous source, as an example of compromising national security. That source,
Status
reported, was Vice-President J. D. Vance, on a background briefing, highlighting yet another instance in which the right hand was unaware of what the right hand was doing.
In a Truth Social post announcing the ban, Trump had complained that “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.” This isn’t exactly an accusation of defrauding the public, but it pretty clearly charges the banned organizations with, at a minimum, misleading it. That said, even Trump seemed to know that he was on shaky ground, preëmptively arguing that the U.S. district judge hearing the case, Timothy J. Kelly, whom Trump himself had appointed, was an unfriendly draw for the Administration’s claims.
The ban followed the now familiar path of Trump’s potentially illegal or unconstitutional acts. As with his attempts to slap his name on the Kennedy Center and his effort to overrule the language of the Fourteenth Amendment, by curtailing birthright citizenship, that path typically travels from absurd idea to absurd (but nonetheless concerning) act, to a legal response that becomes another case study in which we evaluate the extent to which the judicial system is capable of reining in the arbitrary impulses of an aspiring autocrat.
Trump’s concerns about the current case, at least in the short term, proved warranted. Shortly after midnight on Thursday, Kelly imposed a fourteen-day suspension of the ban. That morning, the journalists were still denied entry, so Kelly issued a 12:30
p.m.
deadline for compliance, and their access was restored. Meanwhile, China’s President, Xi Jinping, had arrived in Washington for his first state visit in eleven years. Photographers on the scene reported that Trump joked that China has the “friendliest press corps.” (According to Reporters Without Borders, China ranks a hundred and seventy-eighth out of a hundred and eighty nations in press freedom.) That evening, some of the journalists were again denied access.
It’s worth recalling the degree to which this debacle typifies Trump’s political behavior. During the 2016 election, he withheld campaign-event credentials from Univision, BuzzFeed, the Washington
Post
, and
Politico
. During his first term, he routinely blocked critics and news organizations from his Twitter feed, which resulted in a lawsuit and a district-court ruling that his actions were unconstitutional. In 2018, the Administration denied access to Jim Acosta, then a reporter for CNN. (Kelly also ruled in that case, requiring the White House to restore Acosta’s access.) Last year, the White House denied access to the Associated Press, for refusing to defer to Trump’s preferred designation for the body of water generally known as the Gulf of Mexico. In that instance, the district judge Trevor N. McFadden, another Trump appointee, ruled that “under the First Amendment, if the Government opens its doors to some journalists . . . it cannot then shut those doors to other journalists because of their viewpoints.” He added, “The Constitution requires no less.” The President has sued ABC News, the
Wall Street Journal
, CBS News, the Pulitzer Prize Board, the Washington
Post
, and the
Times
, for hundreds of millions of dollars. His behavior cannot be called unexpected at this point. What was noteworthy this time, however, was the way that the press responded.
A month after the 2016 election, Ben Smith, then of BuzzFeed, lamented that few organizations had come to the defense of the outlets blocked during the campaign.
The New Yorker’s
Susan B. Glasser, who was then with
Politico
, noted that it would be “a terrible disservice to our democracy to have the President of the United States in the business of banning reporters.” A decade later, Trump is in that business, yet it is still not standard for news organizations to come to one another’s defense. The A.P. ban didn’t elicit nearly as much reaction. Several organizations sued by Trump opted to settle in cases that they likely could have won. Moreover, the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, the annual gala celebration of the First Amendment, was held in April despite an intimidation campaign directed at some of those correspondents. After the event was disrupted by an armed intruder, the Administration and the association scheduled a July do-over, where Trump delivered a rambling speech indulging seemingly every tangent that sprang to mind, but his contempt remained apparent. The united front that journalists presented last week is significant, even inspiring, but, if history is any predictor, it will not be the last time they will be called on to do so. ♦

epub_13.title: Are Public Spaces Really for the Public?
epub_13.text:
Are Public Spaces Really for the Public?
In the Streets
Are Public Spaces Really for the Public?
A group of locals is trying to reclaim city spots for the people—including lobbying to turn vacant lots into gardens and fighting the event venue Guastavino’s over a courtyard.
By Parker Henry
September 26, 2026
“In New York City, the streets are your living room,” Jack Espel said the other day, at a coffee shop on East Fifty-ninth Street. Espel, a middle-school history teacher, is part of a group of Midtown East residents who are organizing to transform what they call “derelict parks” into cheery public spaces. That day, they’d met to discuss their goal of turning two dilapidated lots into pocket parks.
Sean Basinski, a semi-retired lawyer who heads the group, was at the center of a recent local kerfuffle: Guastavino’s, a seven-thousand-square-foot event venue situated under the ramp to the Queensboro Bridge, had been treating a small park out front as its private property—roping it off and shooing away pedestrians. “During
COVID
, I brought some kettlebells over to do a workout, and the guard kicked me out,” Basinski said. Later, he tried to use the plaza as a backdrop to photograph some shoes he was selling on eBay, and was again told to leave. “We had words,” he said.
“I did some digging and found out that the park belongs pretty obviously to the City of New York,” Basinski said. He filed a class-action lawsuit against Guastavino’s, alleging “brazen and illegal seizure of public space” and stating that, on a “nearly daily basis,” Guastavino’s evicts the “general public from a public plaza” by selling and marketing “exclusive access to . . . their ‘private garden.’ ” Guastavino’s swiftly removed the “Private Property” signs.
Parks are few and far between in midtown. “We’re park-starved,” Basinski said.
Justin Nuttall, a data manager who grew up nearby, was at the coffee-shop meeting. He described leaving the neighborhood for the first time as a child: “We went to Brooklyn as a family, and I remember being afraid of the grass because I didn’t know what it was.”
Susan Blackwell, a retired copywriter who lives on Sutton Place, chimed in. “My husband grew up on Fortieth and Third, and they used to walk the dog in Grand Central,” she said. “I don’t think he saw a leaf until he went to camp.”
“It’s so uncool to live here that it’s cool,” Nuttall said. “My wife laughed when I told her I grew up in Midtown East.”
Anna Arima, an event planner who moved from Ukraine, has lived in midtown for twelve years. “I used to work for the mayor in Kyiv, which used to be the greenest city in Ukraine,” she said. “When I moved here, I was looking for a way to beautify the community the way we did in Kyiv.” Her super had told her about Basinski’s group.
Others joined after seeing signs Basinski had posted by vacant lots in the neighborhood. “
DOES THIS LOOK GOOD TO YOU
?” one read, next to renderings of what the space could become.
Nuttall had done the visuals. “I just messed around with A.I.,” he said.
The group went to look at the space that was on the day’s agenda: two neighboring lots—fenced off and locked—that span Fifty-ninth Street between First and Second Avenues. All that was there was a dirty tennis ball, a few patches of grass, and a crushed beer can. Kevin Eerkes, a member of the group, stopped as he was jogging by. He removed an AirPod. “The pigeons love these lots,” he said. “And we could, too!”
The group members nodded. As for what the lots should become, Nuttall said, “Well, that has to be crowdsourced when the city finally lets us do something.”
“We’re thinking industrial chic!” Blackwell said. Other ideas were floated: a dog run, an outdoor café.
“Literally just some green for people to lounge on,” Basinski said. “The goal is to get the city to spend the money to turn this into something other than a dump.”
Two years ago, Basinski had had a call with a commissioner at the Department of Transportation, which is responsible for one of the lots. (The spot is a vestige of the Queensboro Bridge’s construction. Originally, tenement buildings stood there.) “He acknowledged the city is not using the space well,” Basinski said. Another D.O.T. rep recently claimed that the lot can’t be repurposed for the public at all. Basinski’s group has collected nine hundred signatures to support the cause. The next step is a meeting with the Community Board. “We’re finally on Board 8’s agenda for next month’s meeting,” he said.
The group was buoyed by a recent local success story. “Did you hear about the Hunter students?” Espel asked. He was referring to the college kids who, in July, had lobbied the city to turn a half block of curb space on East Sixty-ninth Street, by Hunter College, into what they called a “vibrant public gathering space.”
“It’s essentially a few parking spots that the city’s going to let them put some chairs on,” Espel said, dismissively.
“Parking spaces are hallowed,” Blackwell reminded him.
The midtown group has its haters. “Some people say that, if the lots are converted, no one’s going to want to sit there,” Basinski said. “It’s right next to the bridge. It’s noisy.” He went on, “But we’re all already here, next to the bridge. I’m breathing this air, hearing this noise. Let’s at least make it nice.” ♦

epub_14.title: More Sunshine with Joey Arias and Basil Twist
epub_14.text:
More Sunshine with Joey Arias and Basil Twist
Twist Again Dept.
More Sunshine with Joey Arias and Basil Twist
The performance artist and the puppeteer are reviving their avant-garde cabaret show, a leggy fantasia beloved by Cyndi Lauper and the late Paul Reubens.
By Sarah Larson
September 28, 2026
Recently, at the
HERE
Arts Center, near SoHo, the puppeteer Basil Twist, the performance artist Joey Arias, and six unseen puppeteers (“They’re wearing black velvet, hood on, like ninjas,” Twist said) were rehearsing the grand finale of “Arias with a Twist,” their cabaret fantasia from 2008. To the zingy “You Gotta Pull Strings,” from “The Great Ziegfeld,” puppet chorus girls in feathers and fish-nets exited the stage, a Mylar curtain opened, and Arias—Bettie Page bangs, sheer top, Adidas pants—entered, sprawled on a Twistian three-layer cake with showgirls’ legs extending from it like flower petals. Mirrors appeared, the music intensified, and King Kong-size showgirl calves stepped in from stage left and stage right. Meanwhile, the cake wiggled uncertainly. Twist called out, “Can we pause?” He crouched in front of the cake, raising its white fabric frosting. “How can we help?” he asked.
“Hmm,” the cake said. After they chatted, Twist stood. “Let’s take it from the Mylar curtain!” Triumph: the cake spun like a top, its legs high-kicking in unison. Arias, blissful, waved his own legs in the air.
The Center’s theatre, named for Twist’s grandmother Dorothy B. Williams, is underground; upstairs, Twist and Arias talked about the revival. “It feels fantastic,” Arias, who wouldn’t disclose his age (“I like to round up to a hundred”), said. “It’s, like, more sunshine, more happiness. It is never, like, ‘Oh, it’s too much beauty! Too much art!’ ”
Twist, who is fifty-seven, said that they’d written the show quickly, after
HERE
, Twist’s artistic home, had a sudden cancellation. He’d approached Arias, who had just returned from Las Vegas after an eight-year stint starring in Cirque du Soleil’s “Zumanity.” Arias, a fan of Twist’s productions, was game. “Every time I saw Basil, I was, like, ‘Put me in the show!’ ” he said. They wrote it together. “He goes, ‘What do you want to do?’ ” Arias recalled. “I said, ‘Get abducted by aliens, go on an acid trip, and have a Busby Berkeley finale with a big cake!’ ” They riffed on themes for Arias’s return: A desert? Dalíesque Surrealism? Ooh, a jungle?
“We got a whole bunch of donated green fabric, and there was suddenly a jungle,” Twist said. “Corduroy, velvet, cotton, silk.”
The two friends met in the mid-nineties, through Twist’s then boyfriend, whom Arias had met while working at a boutique. “Everybody went to Fiorucci!” Arias said. “This beautiful blond guy—hot pants in the summertime, skating, like, wow!—goes, ‘I’m Bobby Miller. I’m a photographer.’ ” One night, at the club Jackie 60, “Bobby said, ‘I want to introduce you to my boyfriend, Basil Twist.’ ”
Twist said, “Bobby introduced me to a whole world of night life. I had just returned to New York from puppet school in France.” (Twist was the first American to graduate from l’École Nationale Supérieure des Arts de la Marionnette.) He first came to
HERE,
with Miller, for “a gay country-Western cabaret called ‘Y’all.’ Bobby was doing his poetry, and I did a little puppet show,” he said. “Later, I did a bigger project here with Mabou Mines. And the Halloween parade also starts outside these doors! By the way, this year, Joey’s going to be the grand marshal.”
“The daughter of darkness!” Arias said. “I’m representing what the avant-garde, what art, stands for, and that it’s thriving and it’s alive. It’s going to be beautiful.”
Twist and Arias first performed together at a launch party for the fashion publication
MAO MAG
. “I have these marionettes of my grandfather’s on display in the case outside the theatre,” Twist said. His grandfather, a bandleader, had several bandleader puppets—Harry James, Cab Calloway, Paul Whiteman, Arturo Toscanini, and Ted Lewis, each playing an instrument. “I thought, I’ll use these puppets for Joey, because I love him.” On a little stage, “they came alive with Joey flirting with them, playing with them.” The puppets return in the revived “Arias with a Twist,” and the chemistry remains.
Another creative factor was Thierry Mugler, who had designed costumes for “Zumanity” in the early two-thousands. Arias said, “He came with me to see Basil and started to sketch the little nude corset with the little velvet bikini: ‘This is the way you should look.’ ”
The show delighted and astounded many. “Paul Reubens and I were good friends,” Arias said. “He came, and the whole time he was like this”—gobsmacked. “Afterward, he said, ‘Joey, I hate you.’ That meant ‘I love you.’ I said, ‘I know, I hate ya, too. May I introduce you to Basil Twist?’ And immediately he wrapped himself around Basil and the rest of us.” Twist later worked with Reubens on his 2010 Broadway version of “The Pee-wee Herman Show”: Chairry, Globey, and the gang live onstage.
At the revival’s first preview at
HERE
, Twist greeted the audience and pointed out emergency exits, and a New York-accented audience member yelled, “Like a
airplane!
” This turned out to be another Friend of Pee-wee, Cyndi Lauper. After the show, she embraced Arias. “The one and only!” she said. ♦

epub_15.title: Detecting Notes of . . . Citi Field?
epub_15.text:
Detecting Notes of . . . Citi Field?
Tasting Dept.
Detecting Notes of . . . Citi Field?
In the parking lot outside a Mets game, the TikTok sommeliers Ryan and Chris Goydos, of SuperVinoBros, crack open a mystery wine and guess its provenance.
By Arthur Holland Michel
September 28, 2026
On a moonless Friday night at Citi Field, Ryan Goydos, one half of the popular social-media account known as SuperVinoBros, stood at a security entrance reserved for staff, press, mascots, players, and eminences, waiting for his fraternal twin brother, Chris, the other half of the bros, to arrive.
Like the Mets, wine is in a rut. Globally, people drank about a billion fewer gallons of it last year than they did in 2007. The industry has not adapted to the social-media era. The SuperVinoBros, who post fun, peppy videos about their drinking adventures, are determined to change that.
The brothers have close to four hundred and fifty thousand followers across Instagram and TikTok, hailing largely from a young demographic that’s often wary of wine and its stuffy traditions. The renowned sommelier Aldo Sohm is a fan.
Wine Enthusiast
, a magazine of the Old Guard, named the bros “Rising Stars” for 2026. Clips of their exploits have been watched tens of millions of times.
At Citi Field, Ryan had already spent two hours filming content. Inside the stadium’s Cadillac Club, he had tried a lobster roll with a Sauvignon Blanc that made him scrunch his nose (off camera). Chris, a surgical resident at a New Jersey hospital who joins his brother on his days off, had been held up performing a right hemicolectomy on a gunshot victim. He had been working since 6
A.M
.
“Sorry I was late,” Chris said, when he arrived.
“Bro,” his bro replied. “You were saving lives.”
On the concourse, a young man in a black Francisco Lindor jersey dapped the brothers. Their most popular videos are their blind tastings. In traditional blinds, dour sommeliers in waistcoats sniff out the differences between cuvées grown a few miles apart in Burgundy’s Côte d’Or. The brothers usually blind in Chris’s living room, in New Jersey, often while wearing hoodies.
The bros settled into their seats at the bottom of the seventh. They filmed their first blind in 2024. “We always talked about whether it would be easy or not,” Chris said.
It was not easy. That first time, Ryan broke the cork, and Chris guessed way off.
“I was, like, ‘Oh, we shouldn’t post this,’ ” Ryan recalled, sipping an Allagash White. “And Chris was, like, ‘Dude, no. We should absolutely post it.’ ”
The video did well. “It started a very fruitful losing streak,” Chris, who was also drinking beer, said.
The brothers have since filmed around seventy-five blinds. Naturally, they keep score. Ryan has nailed it three times. Chris has clocked either the region or the variety (“half points”) eight times.
The game ended—Mets 2, Marlins 5. The bros headed to the parking lot. They had hoped to shoot a blind in the clubhouse, or in a box. Absolutely not, they had been told. Instead, they set up in the red glow of the tail-lights of a Lexus hybrid owned by Chris’s wife, Akanksha. “We’re at Citi Field right now, blind tasting,” Ryan said into his phone.
He popped the bottle, which was tucked into a lime-green athletic sock, and poured red wine into two plastic cups.
“Oh, shit—it’s the cops,” Chris said. A squad car pulled up, then rolled on. The brothers’ faces caught a blue flicker.
Scientists believe that the hundreds of olfactory receptors in a human nose can discern more than a trillion distinct scents. “It’s got this blueberry, raspberry, light-berry vibe to it,” Chris said, sniffing thoughtfully.
Out of frame, Ryan’s girlfriend, Carolina Mahedy, a former sommelier at Le Bernardin, nosed a glass. “Blinding is like walking down a hallway where all the doors are open,” she had said earlier.
To a novice taster, sipping out of a plastic Mets carafe, the wine smelled like dry grass and very ripe blackberries. Syrah, perhaps?
Mahedy closed her eyes. “This is Cabernet Franc,” she whispered.
Chris sucked air through his teeth. “If it was gonna be a French red, I’d call it a Cab Franc from the Loire Valley.” A 7 train rattled by. He sipped again. “It could be, like, a California Pinot.” He shone his phone’s light through the cup to check for the brown tinge of a Nebbiolo. “Nah, that’s pretty red,” he said. “So I will call this a Pinot Noir from California.”
Ryan handed his brother the bottle. “So, this is—”
Chris yanked off the sock and blinked at the label.
“—a Cab Franc from the Loire Valley!”
Mahedy nodded.
“Fuck! Fuuuck!” Chris looked at his brother. If he had stuck with his original guess, he’d have hit his first homer.
“You were really close!” Ryan said. He cackled.
“Call it the yips,” Chris said.
As the lot emptied, the brothers stuck around to savor the wine. Ryan had just returned from a trip to Bordeaux with Jimmy Butler, the Golden State Warriors’ wine-obsessed forward (record: half a point on one blind). They had put up shots on a hoop at Cos d’Estournel. But blinding out of plastic in Queens, Ryan thought, was just as special.
“Wine is the ultimate social medium,” Chris observed. Everyone nodded.
It was nearing midnight. Chris had to be back at the hospital in six hours. The bottle was almost finished. The bros were drinking to the lees. ♦

Hockey Dads and Hockey Sons
Personal History
Hockey Dads and Hockey Sons
Parenting is a practice. You learn from your mistakes and then repeat them anyway.
By Nick Paumgarten
September 28, 2026
We walked single file through the snow to Lasker Rink, escorted by the coaches. Central Park at night, 1977: in the swirl of a storm, the Park was desolate and pristine. I was eight and had been invited to start skating with the older boys at school. I’d had hockey on the brain for a year, and yet had never really gone to a hockey practice. The Zamboni did a quick dry sweep while we suited up, and then we spilled through the gate onto the ice. Someone dumped out a milk crate full of pucks. I’d never seen such abundance—they may as well have been gold ingots. We scooted and stickhandled around one another, the clatter of our sticks and the rip of our blades muffled by the storm. Whatever anxiety I’d felt about getting out there with the older kids gave way to a saucer-eyed vigilance, the air as bracing as a hit of smelling salts.
Mr. Mila was the hockey coach. His full name was Miloslav Pospisil. He’d been in the Czechoslovak Army and had played on the Czech national hockey and soccer teams. The story we were told was this: One day on the street, in 1968, after the Soviet invasion in response to the Prague Spring, he saw a Soviet soldier shoot a woman who had refused to remove a flower pinned to her overcoat—a rose, the unofficial Czechoslovak national flower. Mila rushed home and told his wife to pack up, and they made their way to the border, then on to Montreal and, later, to New York.
Mila had a military crewcut and a perpetual look of disdain for us kids. We knew him from gym class and were terrified of him. If you horsed around, he pulled you out of the herd and lifted you up by the hair and skin behind your ear. He called this Depozit. He had hoisted boys clear off the ground, sneakers dangling. On the ice, he wore red sweatpants and old skates, and used a stick with a straight blade, no curve at all. He had big thighs and took powerful strides and barked at us with a Slavic severity that we associated with Russian movie villains. An undercurrent of irony, of playacting, went over our heads.
I was the only third grader on the team. A month into the season, I was asked to join the other kids at a peewee tournament upstate. Peewees were eleven and twelve years old. Clearly, they needed bodies. This would be my first-ever organized hockey game. The day before the tournament, at practice, an older kid caught me with a wrist shot to the front of the ankle. It could not have been very hard—we were young and not strong—but a puck, when it hits you right, can leave a welt. That night, the ankle swelled up, and, abuzz with worry and excitement, I hardly slept.
We left the city before dawn. Ninety minutes later, in the locker room, I was having trouble tying my skates. The top of the laces, where you tugged them tight, was right on the bruise. My father gave it a go, hauling on the laces, and I yelped. I was young, I was tired, I was crushed, I was soft. And so I began to cry. Mr. Mila came over and watched me for a while. “You are crybaby!” he said. He told me to take off my skates and get out of the locker room: “You no play.”
Who was more humiliated, my father or me? He took me up to the lounge, overlooking center ice, where a woman offered me a doughnut. He kept his distance in such a way that I sensed his disappointment, in spite of his words of reassurance and some grumbling about Mila. No one likes a crybaby. With the other parents, my face a mess of powdered sugar and dried tears, I watched the first round through a layer of glass and a scrim of shame, and I didn’t get back into the lineup that day. I’d have to wait a while to play my first hockey game.
Ice was scarce in the city. We didn’t have frozen ponds or back-yard rinks. No lawns to flood and obsess over in the Canadian-dad way. There wasn’t much artificial ice, either, at least considering the size of the town and the number of inhabitants. Skating was a novelty, a birthday-party gimmick, like bowling. Once or twice a year, you might find yourself clomping around on crappy rental blades at Rockefeller Center, mesmerized by girls in wool leggings.
Now and then on weekends and vacations, our parents sneaked my brother, Xander, and me onto a brackish Long Island pond, my father in faded flared jeans, a red sweater, and a down vest—a tall man even taller on skates. His were brown leather hockey skates, their steel blades speckled with rust: the hockey equivalent of a leather football helmet. I was transfixed by them, as if they were a pair of pistols.
There was also street hockey, roller hockey, floor hockey. Floor hockey was played at school, in gym class, with plastic sticks and a lightweight orange plastic puck. The walls were padded, allowing for bloodless contact. Mr. Mila presided, severe and disapproving. It was a rare treat in gym to get floor hockey instead of dodgeball or gymnastics. Even now, if I picture the nets and the rolling laundry bin of sticks, I feel a little trill of excitement, like a memory of a circus or an ice-cream truck.
After school, we played street hockey in our shoes, with a ball for a puck, on the uneven paving stones of the plaza where East Eighty-sixth Street comes to an end in Carl Schurz Park. One on one, two on two, five on five: to get a pass off the wall at one end we called out “M.J.!,” for Michael Jackson, after the album “Off the Wall” came out.
Sometimes on weekends, my father played with us. One morning, two older kids on banana-seat bikes cornered a few of us playing street hockey in the park. One of them grabbed our ball and threw it into a fenced lot, which led to a flimsy standoff:
“That’s our ball!”
“Yeah?”
“Go get it!”
“You gonna make me?”
And so on. We had hockey sticks, and so had the means to make them, but that calibre of action—any kind of real bloodshed—was beyond our reckoning or appetite.
I saw my father striding our way with a stick in hand. The big kids, perched on their banana seats, had their backs to him. I gave the bigger one a shove that failed to knock him off his bike. He rebalanced and wound up to throw a punch, but my father caught him by his hoodie and yanked him down to the pavement. He made the kid scale the fence and fetch our ball. It was good to have an enforcer in the family.
You might say we were cake-eaters. That’s what the working-class hockey kids in Minnesota and Michigan call the prep-school swells. I was reared on the Upper East Side of Manhattan. Co-op apartment, private school, Wall Street dad: very cake-y. One can, and I often do, parse how much I was of it and not of it. I indulge in the narcissism of small differences. The euphemism of the era was “upper middle class.” My parents had come to New York from Philadelphia the year before I was born, so, privileged as they were, and connected by birth and education to people of influence and means, they didn’t feel like gilded New Yorkers. The high-society rituals—benefits, dancing schools, clubs—weren’t theirs or mine. Not yet, anyway.
During the week, my father travelled to the heartland to advise regional banks on their mergers with other regional banks. He came back with regional-bank swag, the pencils and rulers I used to do my homework. Around town, people sometimes mistook him for a movie star, and he liked that. Out on the street, after we’d seen “Greystoke” at the Ziegfeld, another moviegoer pointed at him and said, “Yo! It’s Tarzan!” His firm took out an ad in the
Times
with a full-length photograph, shot by Richard Avedon, of my father in a suit. Afterward, his office phone lit up with inquiries from women across the country in need of some corporate finance.
I was, in many ways, a sensitive kid, a good boy. Yet there was something ornery in me, some cussed streak. I’m not sure where it came from, but it was hockey that touched it off, starting around the age of ten. Nothing else made me so assertive, combative, or self-righteous, or brought me so much animal joy. It was an altered state, a kind of goblin mode. I wanted the puck, or the ball or roll of electric tape or whatever doodad was standing in for a puck. I was almost frightened by my hunger to have it and to do things with it, and by the sense of swagger that swept over me when I managed to do the things with it that I wanted to, and by the frustration that coursed through me when I did not.
There was something, perhaps, about the geometry of the game, about finding order amid chaos. And, then, there was another kind of order, a whole alternate ethos that consumed me, an idea of fairness and reprisal. “Do that again and I’ll—” I didn’t know what I’d do, or even what I wanted to do, but an urge to redress certain wrongs took hold. One day, during a street-hockey game, a kid from down the block started pushing my brother around, and I knocked him to the ground and stood over him, poised to throw a punch. I’d surprised myself as much as I had him. With a hockey stick in hand, I could be both artist and vigilante, ace and goon.
Two years after he called me a crybaby, Mr. Mila decided that he no longer wanted to coach the games. My father took over. To the rest of the team, he became, and would ever remain, Coach P. He had played a bit of hockey growing up. The lore is scant: One time, as a boy, he played in a game in Philadelphia. He was wearing figure skates, which in itself seems disqualifying. Grace Kelly—local girl, movie star, now a princess—was in the stands. My father, at some point, found himself on a breakaway. Just him, in open ice, bearing down on the goalie. He caught the serrated point of the figure-skating blade on the ice and fell on his face. Toe pick. We hoard our childhood humiliations and dispense them with care. He played in prep school but quit after three years. He hated having to shovel the rink.
Coach P. paced the bench in a double-breasted navy overcoat over a down vest with brown wide-wale corduroys, hiking boots, ski gloves. The other boys were afraid of him, perhaps in a playful way. If you floated around, he called you a “drifter,” or worse. It must have been something for Mr. Utsch to hear Coach. P. yell out to his eleven-year-old son, “Utsch, you’re a pussy!” Xander and I knew that his fits of anger were fearsome but harmless, as did the others who’d spent time around our family. Behind the bench, the hard-assery was more gag than threat. The Great Santini with a touch of Chevy Chase.
He didn’t know much about the game’s finer points. He was not, as they say, an X’s and O’s guy. He said, “Forecheck, back-check, paycheck” and “My way or the highway.” His coinages, we thought. His highest compliment, the opposite of a drifter, was “hustler.” I endeavored to be one.
He wrote out the lineup in his left-handed script, in blue ink, on swatches of graph paper. He carried it around the days before our games and showed it to my brother and me. Here was a grownup—a man’s man, who came home at night from an office tower wearing a tailored suit and invited us into his walk-in closet, which held his executive clothes, his leather belt and English-leather lace-ups, the cedar shoe trees and horsehair brushes and jars of cordovan polish—caring so sincerely about, and devoting so much time to, an undertaking that, although it meant the world to me, even then I knew to be utterly trivial. It struck me that he knew my friends’ tendencies, that he had a sense of our hierarchies and skills, that he thought more of the better players and less of the weaker. I pictured him at his desk on Wall Street folding a sheet of graph paper into four quarters and writing out the names of eleven-year-old kids. It was flattering and unnatural, and it provided a first shudder in my perception of him as an infallible giant.
In the summer of 1982, I aged out of Coach P.’s squad. Eighth grade, thirteen: bantams. I signed up for a house league in the Bronx, rostering with a team from Pelham, just over the county line. We wore purple and yellow, like the Marcel Dionne Los Angeles Kings. I knew no one. Here was my first locker room rife with talk of jerking off and getting laid. I kept quiet, off and on the ice. Puberty hadn’t hit me yet. Jerking off, to say nothing of getting laid, was as yet a rumor. My shifts on the ice came and went, rarely with any consequence. The games were rougher than I was used to. I shied away from trouble and became a perimeter player. My father came home early from work to drive me to the Bronx and back. He watched from the corner. I could sense the disappointment, the boredom, his reassessing the worthiness of the sacrifice. I saw myself through his eyes and didn’t like what I saw.
About halfway through the season, I tried to avoid a check and got clipped in the leg, knee on knee. The knee swelled and stiffened. By the time it got better, the schedule was all but done. I doubt the coach missed me.
There wasn’t any burning preconception that our two boys would play hockey, or, for that matter, become anything in particular. My wife, Siv, and I were open to whatever might come, or so we told ourselves. We weren’t yet, and would probably never fully be, aware of the expectations and received ambitions that we projected onto the boys. The older one was Oli, pronounced with a long “O,” like the Finnish player Olli Jokinen. On his third birthday, in the fall, we gave him his first pair of skates, Bauers no bigger than my fists.
“Do you know what day it is?” his mother asked.
“Hockey!” he said.
And so it was that he spent many days that winter at public sessions and on frozen ponds, puttering around with a chair or a held hand, and this may be proof that I was, and am, not being honest with myself. To call the pull of the ice gravitational would be an abrogation of agency. I wielded the magnet, whether I meant to or not. I was the one who saw something edifying in it all, who imbued playing a game with the making of a man. I was the one who made arguments on behalf of pushing through exhaustion and pain, of showing up even when you didn’t feel like it.
It wasn’t that I believed myself to be so staunch; I wasn’t a marine or a monk or even an athlete of any distinction. I’d quit in high school, fed up with playing for other men—the coaches, my father. Or so I imagined. I was on to and into other things, whatever the opposite of sports was. Books, music, pot—a demented life of the mind. In time, I came back to hockey. It was a relapse, of a kind. Roller hockey, intramural hockey, men’s league.
The boy coached by his father was now the father coaching his sons. I knew, as much from failure as from absorption, that if hockey was good for anything it was for its lessons of forbearance. Maybe my boys, if I handled them right, would turn out sturdier than me.
When Oli turned five, we got him the full kit. I went to Cosby’s, the bedraggled hockey store next to Madison Square Garden, and bought the smallest pads I could find. In the apartment, I helped him tug on gear and tighten straps with the brisk tenderness of a veterinarian tending to a sedated pet. His excitement, visible behind the lattice of the face mask, was intoxicating, the pride of a novitiate. The extent to which even this kind of innocent dress-up is a means of indoctrination—the knottiness of this early gender programming—is leavened or perhaps obscured by its adorableness. He bumped around the house, proud and almost delirious with his transformation, and with the cognizance that he might be pleasing his father. The armor both emboldened him and somehow sapped him of strength, as though the plastic exoskeleton had drawn starch from his bones. After a few minutes, he lay on the floor with arms out and legs splayed, and looked up at the ceiling, daydreaming of who knows what. Every frozen pond has one, a distrait child squinting into the sky, making angels of the ice shavings. Here, in the one-and-a-half-bedroom apartment, was ours.
I signed Oli up for a local hockey program called the Mighty Mites, coached by a guy I played beer-league hockey with. Oli showed up a few times, bumped around on the ice with the other kids, but then one day in the locker room, perhaps cowed by the bluster and chatter of the dads, he refused to get ready for practice. I pleaded, he held fast. In a panic, I called my wife. She said to let him be.
“But he made a commitment,” I said.
“He did not make a commitment,” she said. “He is five.”
That was it for the Mighty Mites. But he took up hockey again the following year, as a kindergartner at a new school, the one I’d attended. His class practiced on Friday afternoons at Lasker. I volunteered as an assistant coach, which meant being out there as an errand boy and horsing around with the kids. It was as casual as could be, a romper room on ice. More than half the kindergarten class had joined the program. Most of them couldn’t even get dressed in the gear, much less skate. Some came with their mothers, very few with their fathers, and a lot of them with nannies, South Asians and West Indians, who lugged or wheeled their charges’ bags of gear. I roamed the locker room and helped with the pads and the laces. To see, or try to see, these little princelings through their babysitters’ eyes made the whole thing seem a bit ridiculous, if not insidious. The idea was to toughen up the kids, teach them some self-reliance, yet here they were, attended by their handmaids.
Before practice, as the Zamboni made its rounds, the boys piled up behind the door to the ice, jostling for position. After a moment—the sanctified fermata of waiting for the new layer of water to freeze—a coach unlatched the door and they tumbled onto the ice, not one remaining on his skates. The pads, the helmets, the sticks, the bounded ring: it was all a pretext for roughhousing. No one discouraged it.
I was happy that my boy was skating and enjoying it, and was immediately eager for him to do it more. Where did this come from? Was it keeping up with the Joneses or meeting some idea of an athletic standard instilled by my father? Was it a resurrection of my thwarted ambitions for myself? Which is to say, was I living through my child? Of course I was.
It wasn’t long before Oli joined a travel-hockey program. Day One was at a rink in a mall up the pike, in New Rochelle. This was mini-mites, five- and six-year-olds, mostly, the smallest of the small. We drove up at daybreak, Oli in back, still in a booster seat. When we got to the rink and he started dressing, I could see the trepidation and doubt in his eyes. Older kids strutted around in their pads. Their dads made a caffeinated ruckus. I tried, in Oli’s presence, to convert the boisterousness and swagger of the others into cheerfulness, but I could sense that he knew I was forcing a mood. This never worked with him. Something gave way, some dismay set off by the jersey he was given or the number he’d chosen or the bravado of the other children or the merrymaking of the parents or the nervous exhilaration of his dad—those first-day heebie-jeebies, one’s own memory of which persists deep in the bones. He refused to go on the ice, and he wept. My moonfaced boy, wrecked somehow by a disconnect between what he’d wanted and what this was, dug in. Other dads sidled up and tried to coax and reassure him, but, if I couldn’t, they didn’t stand a chance. We sat awhile. Limbo. My heart ached for the boy, yet the task at hand was to get him onto the ice and into the program. The striving, the striving. He sat on a bench, his tiny legs not even reaching the floor. I left him alone for a while and stood at the glass watching the session, my soul a twist of sympathy, frustration, embarrassment, and even something like fear—that he might be too sensitive for this world, too
soft
—and the realization that I might feel this way about sensitivity, about the proper mettle in a boy, made me ashamed, too, so the brain, the self-justifying cortex, whichever lobe that is, got to work formulating arguments on behalf of my impatience and stipulations, to override the shame.
The mood passed, and he eventually stood up and skated out onto the ice and made his fleeting impression and got sorted into a group that wasn’t the top group.
Once you spent some time on the ice with the younger kids, you realized quickly that maybe one out of three of them had the ability to cultivate a sense of strategy and structure. There were those who just chased the puck and those who ignored it. You had your blinded bulls and your daisy sniffers, your Ratóns and your Ferdinands. It was hard enough for a lot of the kids to stand in line, maintain eye contact, keep from crying. The capacity for abstraction and awareness didn’t necessarily align with intelligence or skill. Spatial awareness, hockey sense—maybe it was a cast of mind.
Still, parents had a hard time letting go of the idea that their tyros were miniature professionals. A year later, I began helping coach the mini-mites, who now included my younger son, James. The head coach, from Calgary, Alberta, had been a star college player and had had a couple of stints in the American Hockey League, the best of the minor leagues. Now retired and starting a career in finance, he was more or less a volunteer, and the seriousness of the parents at this paltry level of ours astonished and amused him. But, with that western-Canadian knack for self-possession, he revealed none of this to the constituents. The day after Halloween, he arrived a half hour late for a 7
A.M.
Saturday practice and stepped onto the ice reeking of booze, with smeared lipstick on his collar and white Dracula face paint on his neck. I fetched a towel and tidied him up—what else are assistant coaches for?
A Sunday game in Queens, at dawn, Dracula and me behind the bench: Our mini-mites wobbled around a full sheet of ice like grapeshot on a dinner plate. There were lines painted under the ice—blue, red—but none of the kids had any idea what they signified. Once the referee dropped the puck, the parents in the stands shouted at their kids.
Go! Skate! Get it! Shoot!
After the game—a loss, according to the scoreboard—a father came up to me to complain that our players seemed not to have a grasp of proper positioning on the breakout. I was new enough to it all, and I understood that this was preposterous. But it wouldn’t be long before I would forget and be tricked into expecting too much. Something came awake in me, an incubus of ambition—a desire for excellence, obviously of a shine that would reflect back on me. The vanity of parenthood took hold.
I hadn’t set out to coach my sons. The earliest impulse was to be on the ice with them. If I was going to go to the rink, I might as well get to skate. I wanted to play with them, not teach them to play, much less to play for me. Still, it was pride, of a kind, that drew me to the bench. A sense that I knew something about the game, that I could be a nurturing or at least an entertaining adjunct to the professional coaching staff. Most of the coaches were Czech, a new generation of Mr. Milas. My father, when he took over, had embodied a sense of hockey—and life!—as lark, not just as proving ground. But eventually a dad’s tutelage sets in motion the familiar cycle of expectation and disappointment.
The weekends teemed with hockey, each boy with as many as five engagements over the forty-eight hours. Two or three games and a couple of practices at a web of rinks, back and forth across toll bridges and state lines. Siv maintained a color-coded hockey calendar that, if you looked at it too long, induced an epileptic fit. She and the other moms had a car pool for the weekday practices, and she was often with one boy when I was with the other, although I strove to be everywhere, to see every shift, and often took her leg of the weekday car pool, since I was supposed to be on the ice coaching anyway. Still, she watched more hockey and huffed more Zamboni fumes and developed more nuanced opinions about it all than she would ever have imagined.
My participation, as driver, dad, coach, manager, crank, and fan, sucked the strength out of me, like going overboard in a wintry sea. The rank refrigerated air, the burnt coffee, the Tastykakes, the cross-chop of excitement and stress and boredom and disgruntlement. By Monday, I was saturated by it all, sallow and hoarse.
On the weeknights, it was my turn to play, on whatever team in whatever league. One night, my father, after a business dinner nearby, dropped by the rink to watch. Beer league means never playing in front of your parents, or anybody at all. So this was an oddity. I experienced a little flutter at the first sight of him, standing in the corner up against the glass. Coach P., in the overcoat. A teammate nudged me on the bench: “Is that your dad?”
It had been a lifetime since he’d appraised me on the ice: a skinny longhaired kid in Pelham purple lost amid the carnage of a bantam game in the Bronx. Now about the age he’d been then, and attuned to his presence, I skated harder than usual. But, when the third period began, I noticed he was gone.
The next morning, I waited for his report. He called in the afternoon. “What did you think?” I asked.
“You guys are terrible!” he said.
I was cocksure enough to find this pronouncement more inaccurate than unkind, needy enough to find it hurtful, and man enough to see the sense in it.
A Sunday 7
A.M.
game at the Playland Ice Casino, in Westchester, versus the Rye Rangers. The kids arrived in darkness and began warming up in the parking lot. The younger you are, the earlier you play. Perhaps it’s to weed out the faint of heart. The kids who learn to wake up at 5:30
A.M.
to play hockey are the same ones who in thirty years will have the fortitude to skate at midnight.
One of my beer-league teammates, a master rigger of industrial cranes, and I were assistant coaches. His son J. and my boy James were teammates and friends as mites. J. was tiny, with long curly hair and goggles like Kareem Abdul-Jabbar’s, and he treated James—who was eight, a year older, tall and wiry, with a blond bowl cut and a volatile streak—as the big brother he didn’t have. The head coach was Lada, a former Czech junior player fresh in town from Kopřivnice. He spoke very little English. He led skating clinics for the kids, designing convoluted edge-work drills that he couldn’t explain. He had J.’s dad and me demonstrate the sequences, then barked at us, half facetiously, when we got it wrong, endearing him to the kids. When James lost his temper on the ice, which was often, Lada bellowed, “Red eyes!,” his term for hot temper, and benched James for several shifts, the son seething while his father, pretending to be objective, tried to ignore him.
That Sunday, it wasn’t yet 8
A.M.
when a Rye player shoved James from behind into the boards. James went down awkwardly and stayed prone a moment, then leaped up and, with an implausible ferocity, cross-checked the other kid in the ear. The Rye boy collapsed to the ice, and the other kids poured in and began grappling with one another, while parents shouted and pointed. Soon there was a pile of mites, with the two referees pulling players off and flinging them aside like puppies. Through the windows, you could see that the sun had risen over the Long Island Sound. I thought of my son’s fellow second graders back in the city, likely still asleep or watching cartoons in their pajamas or getting dressed for church or whatever the unrinked got up to on weekend mornings, but here at Playland my boy had instigated a munchkin brawl.
On the bench, I kept my cool. It can be a matter of pride among hockey men—coaches, executives, scouts—to maintain a poker face when hell breaks loose on the ice. Cross your arms, chew your gum. Act like you’ve seen it before. But inside I was all twisted up. From a certain remove, the mayhem amused me, but I worried, with a dad’s fierce, selfish concern, about James’s well-being—his head, ribs, neck, shoulders—and muttered justifications to myself for the retaliatory stick to the ear. “Kid had it coming,” my inner hockey man said. Yet I also worried about that Rye boy and felt the rustlings of embarrassment, guilt, or even outrage. The refs kicked James out of the game and gave Rye a five-minute power play. They scored twice. It cost us the game.
By then, James was hiccupping back tears alone in the locker room. After a nod from me, a dad in the stands went to look in on him. This man no doubt held me in some way responsible, as both father and coach, for the violence and loss of self-control. I could see it in his expression, in the mixture of sympathy and scorn. I absorbed his judgment, and even though, on entering the locker room, I immediately checked in on James to ask about his head and spine and give his shoulder a surreptitious squeeze—what he really needed was a hug—on the car ride home I began to criticize him for losing his cool, for attempting to hurt another player, and also for putting his team down a player and depriving it of his services. “You can’t keep doing this,” I said. “We need you out there.”
I knew it was bad to talk to James about the game, or really to say anything at all besides “Let’s get some pancakes,” but, because I was wound up myself, or because I felt that I needed to impart some kind of lesson, as a father and as a coach, or because there was some childish part of me that needed to spill my own disquiet onto someone else, I persisted. Sometimes I savored the sweetness of driving to and from the rink with one or the other son in back; other times, I felt like little more than a chauffeur. Today, I was a cop, with a perp in back, behind a scrim of parental expectation as impenetrable as bulletproof glass.
James said nothing. In the rearview mirror, I could see him in his black compression shirt, his hair a sweaty mess, his face red and eyes puffy and cheeks rimed with the salt of his tears. The mood in the car was sour. I had a headache from too little sleep and too much coffee, plus all the griping and yelling—mine and everyone else’s. My coaching jacket smelled like a dead mouse. I took an absent-minded inventory of the right pocket’s contents: whistle, pack of gum, wad of used hockey tape, and my triplicate copy, as team manager, of the score sheet from the game, on which I knew it was written that No. 19, in green, had incurred a major penalty, for cross-checking, and a game misconduct. I wondered about the rules and whether he would be suspended, and then about the possibility that he might welcome the time off. I worked up the grace to suggest that we stop somewhere for breakfast.
One strives to be better. Parenting is a practice. You learn from your mistakes and then repeat them anyway. My father, watching my boys and their teammates from the stands, often criticized the plays they made, or failed to make, and so I felt compelled to defend them, even though those plays and failures often irked me, too.
A couple of years later, James, now ten, was the captain of the team and the top dog on defense. I was coaching the defensemen; I was coaching my son. I stood at their end of the bench, worked the door, called out the pairings, kept an eye on the matchups and the length of the shifts, and chatted with the boys. Sometimes my delivery was playful, jesting, even conspiratorial. (I’ve since been told that it is hurtful to be sarcastic with children.) Other times, I was keen, instructive, even scolding. James, of whom I expected the most, sometimes bore the brunt.
Somehow the tournament semifinal game went to overtime. Sudden death: next goal wins. Early in the overtime, my son and his partner botched a retrieval behind our net, which led to a turnover and a goal. Game over, tournament over. Our boys, dejected, drifted back toward the bench. James’s body language suggested that he blamed his partner. So I pointed at James as he came to the bench, and said, not playfully or jestingly or even conspiratorially, “That was on
you
. That was
your
fault.” I couldn’t take it back. He looked at me with something like disgust, both because he didn’t agree and because he knew that what I’d said was harsh and uncalled for, an instance of an adult betrayal of dignity and comportment.
The following week, I agreed to quit working the bench. I wouldn’t coach James again. It may be that this was when, if perhaps not why, James began to lose interest in the game. He still played, often eagerly and very well, but he had come to resent hockey’s monopolization of his time, and, perhaps, the yoke of expectation. Also, he had discovered basketball: pickup with friends, then the team at school. Basketball! Sacrilege. Out on the hardwood, as an energy guy off the bench, he bounced around with the avidity and glee of a parolee. I took it as a delicious rebuke. Another dad exclaimed, “James is the happiest basketball player on the planet!” ♦
This is drawn from “
The Intangibles
.”
