Narrow Escape
Fiction
Narrow Escape
By Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
September 27, 2026
In 1948, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, who was then twenty-nine and incarcerated in a Soviet facility—serving an eight-year sentence for having criticized Joseph Stalin in his private correspondence—began writing an autobiographical novel titled “Love the Revolution.” The novel, which was never completed, was published in Russia in 1999, and will come out in English for the first time later this year. This passage, adapted from the first chapter of the novel, is set in Rostov-on-Don, in the summer of 1941.
It happened like this. The availability of bread was in a phase of so-called temporary difficulties. There was a crush of many hundreds outside the bread shops. The limit was two kilos per person, and no ration cards had been instituted yet. The family of Gleb Nerzhin’s wife, Nadya, had gone three days without bread, but Gleb had grown up during the first Five-Year Plan and had mastered the art of waiting in line or in a milling crowd, of sprinting and scrounging, so he volunteered to scrounge. This entailed standing in the gateway of one’s housing block while it was still night and waiting for the dawn to break. In every gateway all along the street, similar groups were lining up for the start, casting sidelong glances at one another but not making a run for the bread shop until it was time: after all, for security reasons, no one was allowed out in the streets at night, except for night patrols and policemen. But just as electric charges gradually build up in lead-colored thunderclouds until at last the intolerable difference in potential gives violent birth to lightning, so, too—without any word of command, without a sign or prior agreement, without conscious intent, not even at the moment when dawn became perceptible—somebody stirred, someone else swayed, a third one took a step, and, from every gateway, the crowd surged toward the bread shop, merging into an avalanche. Not every war could boast of attacks like this, with no one needing to be urged on, everyone rushing forward, selflessly giving their all. On reaching the bread shop, this throng was supposed to stretch itself out into a single file, but, writhing noisily, it simply could not manage to do so, since every participant claimed to have arrived before the others. Gleb was in the midst of this seething mass. He had secured one of the first places, next to the wall, and clung with one hand to a projecting brick by the entryway, so that he was neither shoving nor making a din but patiently waiting for the bread delivery in two hours’ time and the shop’s opening in three.
Despite that fact, the policeman who arrived to restore order did not touch those who were pushing and shoving, or even those who were brawling, but picked on none other than Gleb, who stood out, with his lean and haughty, bookish air, among all the barefoot boys, cantankerous grannies, girls, and raucous women. The policeman beckoned to him. Gleb gave a look of surprise. The man then summoned him out loud, calling him “white shirt.” Gleb didn’t move. The policeman began to push aside the crowd, which had quietened down. Gleb stepped forward to meet him, asking what this was all about. The man demanded that Gleb follow him to the police precinct. Gleb made a perfunctory protest but gave in, to avoid creating a scene and being made to look ridiculous. And so they set off.
The precinct was some four long city blocks distant. At first, Gleb felt nothing but irritation at losing his place in the queue; he’d done so well to get it, and it had cost him two hours of sleep. Then, after walking for a couple of blocks, directing withering sneers at the policeman’s reddish face, which was as impassive as that of a stone idol, Gleb cooled down and succumbed to boredom. There was nothing remarkable in any of this; he would be released on the spot at the precinct, but it would be stupid to run into one of his acquaintances in such company.
Read an interview with the author’s son for the story behind the story.
Inside the precinct, there were two men at the desk. The stone idol made his report: “Comrade Lieutenant, this man was inciting panic.”
Gleb began to reply in a rapid, agitated voice. “Listen, Comrade Lieutenant, this is absolute nonsense. I was standing there perfectly peacefully. I wasn’t causing any disturb—”
“You . . . just hold on,” the lieutenant said, squinting at him coldly. “Sit.” And, raising his voice: “Sit over there, farther down!”
“Excuse me, why should I sit? I need to be going!”
“Sit down, I tell you.”
Did no one understand Russian here? Gleb shrugged, sat down on a bench, and began to examine the official furnishings of the duty room with studied inattention: the red calico tablecloth with a big ink stain, the cloudy water jug with a broken-off spout, the filing cabinet whose warped door no longer closed properly, the stacks of files inside it, the duty officer’s fountain pen, which was spattering as he wrote.
Gleb hadn’t waited fifteen minutes when two more policemen came in with another couple of detainees, registering them under the same charges:
—panic-mongering;
—rumor-spreading.
Had Gleb not been a twenty-three-year-old greenhorn philosopher, he would have understood everything by now: that, two days earlier, Stalin had given his incoherent radio speech addressing his “brothers and sisters,” almost adding “in Christ,” which was punctuated by intervals of heavy breathing and the sound of gurgling water; that the new catchwords “panic-mongers” and “rumor-spreaders” had been seized upon; that a corresponding Decree had been promulgated; and that this entailed hunting down the perpetrators, so that yesterday the police had been briefed at a meeting, and today, from first light, they’d been out on their manhunt, making sure that the number of detained suspects listed in their daily reports demonstrated their vigilance and justified their existence. But Gleb’s understanding of things was too complicated for him to be able to grasp anything as plain as that.
Twice more he protested his detention, then at last the man on duty called him forward, noted down his name and address, and released him, promising that he’d be summoned again. At this Gleb merely smiled ironically. It was clear to him, as he emerged from the duty room, with its lingering smell of tobacco smoke, into a fresh and verdant July morning: having found nothing incriminating, they were releasing him for good.
But a day later a smudged violet-ink summons was delivered to his address, stating the time that he was to appear before the investigating officer. This was now so stupid that it wasn’t funny anymore. Gleb could hardly wait for the appointed time, reached the precinct almost at a run, and entered the office, vigorously flicking back his unruly hair—it was time to rid himself of this trivial nonsense, which was clinging to him like a leech. He began impetuously rattling off his incontrovertible arguments, but the junior lieutenant with slicked-down hair who sat at the desk pointed to a chair some way off and busied himself with putting a new nib in his pen, retrieving some bloated scraps from the bottom of his inkwell, and pouring in fresh ink. He then began leafing through his papers. But what papers could there possibly be in a case like this?
Gleb’s ardor waned as the minutes passed and he ran out of words to say. Distractedly, he watched as each successive page was turned. After going through two file folders, the investigating officer took out a clean interrogation-record form and, for some reason, examined it against the light, then unhurriedly began to ask his questions: surname, given name, patronymic, date of birth, occupation, home address. To Gleb, it was grotesque that the officer didn’t seem to make the slightest effort to establish the truth but was solely preoccupied with filling out each line as evenly and elegantly as possible—and this in such tempestuous hours, when million-strong armies were clashing in the west, motorized divisions were racing through breaches in the front at a hundred kilometres per hour, whereas, here, there was only the ticking of the clock on the wall and the occasional scratching of an illiterate pen, which, moreover, was investigating a meaningless, insignificant incident. The police lieutenant appeared to be writing down exactly what Gleb was telling him, but relying upon completely different words, with the result that Gleb confirmed the fact of his participation in organizing a queue for bread at 4
a.m.
outside such-and-such bread shop, where he had been detained by a guardian of the law, who had duly escorted him to the precinct. All this was set out in question-and-answer form, without appropriate syntax but with ornate flourishes; was certified at the end by Gleb’s signature; and, together with a copy of Article 206 attesting to the termination of the investigation, was entered into the file, to which the testimony of the policeman involved in the incident had already been attached.
Gleb tried to arrange a meeting with the precinct chief, but this proved impossible, and he emerged onto the street with a depressing sensation that he’d fallen victim to a stupid joke, one that was decidedly unamusing. It was all nothing! Hot air! A scrap of paper! It shouldn’t have any consequences at all, yet it had left an unpleasant taint that soured his mood.
It so happened that Gleb’s wife, Nadya, had promised Ella Dovner, one of Gleb’s old school friends, a gentle, clever girl with large circular-framed glasses, that they’d come and visit her that evening. Everyone had disbanded and scattered so swiftly that they were the only two of Ella’s large circle of friends who could come for the evening, sharing with her the now burdensome luxury of the living room, with its grand piano, plush armchairs, mirrors, and carpets (but no radio receiver, since these had been universally banned in June). The friends tried to guess what the murky future held in store and grieved softly over the past, which was so dear, as they sat, in the gathering dusk, out on the balcony above the main street of the city.
Beautiful Bolshaya Sadovaya, long since renamed Engels Street, ran straight as an arrow and was a clean, tree-lined, and gaudily populous boulevard, freed now from clattering streetcars, the only sounds being the soft swish of automobile and trolleybus tires, and the shuffling of pedestrians’ feet. This, Rostov’s main thoroughfare, wasn’t illuminated by the familiar bright glare of its many street lamps, or by light from its windows, now blacked out, but emerged from the darkness all the more gently in a milky cloak of moonlight. Beneath the balcony, this street, witness to and confidante of the entire twenty-three years of these young people’s lives, was languishing in the fragrant July night, densely thronged with strolling city dwellers even now. The abundance of typically Southern white suits bathed in white moonlight, the leisurely movement of the pedestrian groups, with no one attempting to overtake or jostle others, even the blue lamps at the kiosks selling ice cream and soda water—all this was so festive, so peaceful, so remote from the war that it made one want to pretend for this one evening that there
was
no war, that its jagged shrapnel had not sliced into the tender body of life, that one could still dream of a future, still sit listening to concerts. . . . But no! Even here in the Dovners’ affluent apartment, there was no pretending. Ella’s father himself was due to leave in the next day or two, destined—even he—for the front. From the balcony, the young people could see his car pull up outside.
Dr. Dovner was over forty, and, though he played an important role in the official side of life, he was inwardly quite contemptuous of it, always preferring the practical, material side—that is, things as they really were, and not the way people strove to depict them. This had brought him great success in life. A corpulent, agile man with ruddy cheeks, full of joie de vivre, he easily distinguished worthy individuals from feckless ones, achievers from windbags, and well knew that what was actually done differed greatly from how it was portrayed in writing. He readily entered mutual arrangements of the “You scratch our back, we’ll scratch yours” type, and took timely shelter under the wing of the omnipotent Party: and so, by the spring of 1941, he had become one of Rostov’s most notable personalities—the deputy head of the oblast health department, the director of its biggest clinic, a member of both the oblast and municipal soviets of workers’ deputies—proof of his remarkable skill at combining the functions of doctor, medical administrator, and devoted Communist.
Dovner had only a sketchy idea of who Gleb was, but had noticed him as one of the regulars at the young people’s table when dinners were held in the apartment. And he recognized him now when he came out onto the balcony with the intent of spending some time with his daughter. But Ella, who combined a generous, compassionate heart with an utter lack of understanding of real life, despite the fact that—or perhaps precisely because—she was studying for a post-graduate degree in literature, voiced a complaint to him as he approached, while twirling a flower around her little nose: “Papa! Gleb here didn’t do anything, but they’re summoning him for an investigation, putting together a report. . . .”
Gleb was embarrassed at being made to look like a supplicant. But, when Dovner questioned him lightly about the details, the man’s infectious laughter made Gleb even more convinced that such trifles were hardly worth mentioning at all. They sat on the balcony for a while, chatting, then the doctor called Gleb into the room, without the girls.
Dovner was every inch the civilian, and it was odd to see him already in uniform. The tailor had had his work cut out fitting the soft woollen battle-dress blouse to Dovner’s unathletic and paunchy frame. The broad officer’s belt was buckled on one of the first holes. But, for all that, he cut a rather gallant figure, with three bars gleaming red on the collar tabs on either side of his sturdy neck, and he looked not like a victim of the tumult of war but like a man pleased with a change of occupation and form of dress. He was off to take up command of a field hospital.
In this final day or two before his departure, when Dovner was already free of the cares and concerns of life out of the war zone but not yet burdened with those of the front, his experienced eye was able to grasp the significance of Gleb’s case immediately: “Do you realize what this could mean? Ten years in the camps.”
There is a point beyond which the scale of a threat or a danger ceases to scare us. We might take fright when faced with a bandit drawing his knife, but if he shouts, “I’ll smite you with a hundred lightning bolts,” we’d barely flinch. “Five months” would have frightened Gleb more than “ten years.” But Papa Dovner wasn’t joking. He lowered himself languidly onto the couch, like a performer after too many encores, and with eyes half closed, said, “Children, children, what
do
they teach you at university?”—then nodded toward the telephone directory. “Look up the precinct you were at. The chief’s office.”
“Now? But it’s evening,” Gleb demurred uncertainly.
“They work nights, it goes with the job,” Dovner said, narrowing his eyes. “Just look it up.”
“Do you really know him, too?” Gleb asked, hastily leafing through the directory.
“Easier to ask me whom I
don’t
know. All the commanding heights must be in the hands of the proletariat. I could order you a plane right now to fly you to the Far East. I could put you in charge of a restaurant. Or reserve a prenatal bed in a sanatorium for pregnant women—would you like that? What’s that number? Zero-five-three-eight-four?”
The magisterial way he dialled, still slouched back on the sofa, using one chubby white finger, never turning the dial all the way around but just far enough for each number to register, all while holding the receiver in the same hand—even minutiae such as these bespoke a man who held the commanding heights in this city of half a million inhabitants.
“Hello? Am I speaking to the Fourth Department? Captain Maksimov? Doctor Dovner here. . . . Hello, there. . . . How’s it going? Me, too. . . . And what little matter would that be? That’s fine, we’ll run it through the Medical Assessment Board. Send it along, and I’ll alert the Deputy Head. . . . Me? I’m off to the front. . . . Listen, I’ve got something to ask you, too. Write this surname down . . . ‘Nerzhin’ . . . that’s ‘N’ for ‘November,’ ‘E’ for ‘Echo,’ ‘R’ for ‘Rubbish,’ ‘Zh’— Yes, that’s it. Have you made a note of it? Your boys over there have cooked up a case against him, but it’s just a mistake. . . . Well, all right. . . . Fine, you can call later. . . . Oh, you can check now? Good, go ahead.”
Toying with the receiver not far from his ear, Dovner looked at Gleb, but his thoughts were already elsewhere, deep in his own concerns. And Gleb looked at Lieutenant Colonel Dovner in wonder: the feelings this man aroused were strangely ambivalent. From every theoretical point of view, Dovner was transforming the Soviet system, which had been conceived as something of perfect, crystalline purity. Yet whenever Gleb saw Dovner’s broad smiling face, his quick gaze, expressing not exactly a lofty intellect but a sharp, vigorous, and commodious mind, he could imagine all those disarming, mutually advantageous deals, which always benefitted specific individuals, not so much in terms of enrichment but, rather, in terms of evasion, exemption, dodging responsibility, and Gleb wondered why Dovner, rather than seeming a reprehensible character, could still appear so likable.
“Well? . . . You’ve found it? And the hearing’s already set for the day after tomorrow? Just drop the case, then, all right? So long, then. . . . Yes, yes, we’ll fix it.”
Dovner gently replaced the receiver.
“D’you understand?”
No! Right to the very end, Gleb had not truly understood or sensed the danger he’d been in. Those sensible decrees against panic-mongers that he’d so recently welcomed could not affect
him
, after all! It had so easily passed him by, as if nothing had ever happened: the gigantic wheel had rolled by, almost squashing him to a pulp—yet Gleb could not even grasp that the wheel existed and that it was in motion. ♦
(Translated, from the Russian, by Alexis Klimoff and Michael Nicholson.)
This is drawn from “
Love the Revolution: An Unfinished Novel
.”

epub_28.title: The Unknowable Miley Cyrus
epub_28.text:
The Unknowable Miley Cyrus
Pop Music
The Unknowable Miley Cyrus
The singer has been raunchy, folksy, psychedelic, Disney-clean. On her new album, “Bass Persuades,” she disappears onto the dance floor.
By Amanda Petrusich
September 19, 2026
These days, pop stars are required to participate in a relentless cycle of self-annihilation and triumphant rebirth—with each album, a new Era!—but there’s something almost uncanny about the plasticity of Miley Cyrus. After entering the public consciousness, in 2006, as the chipper, apple-cheeked star of the Disney Channel series “Hannah Montana,” she released multiple songs declaring herself a hedonist, beginning with “Can’t Be Tamed,” in 2010, and reaching a nihilistic apotheosis with her fourth album, “Bangerz,” from 2013. The single “We Can’t Stop” is an unrepentant ode to ripping it up: “So la-da-di-da-di, we like to party / Dancing with Molly / Doing whatever we want,” she announces in the pre-chorus. To some degree, Cyrus’s rebellion was preordained: in 2008, when she was fifteen, Annie Leibovitz photographed her nude, wrapped only in a bedsheet, for the cover of
Vanity Fair
. “You can’t say no to Annie!” Cyrus cheerfully told a reporter.
The Cyrus of “Bangerz” was plucky and impulsive, prone to twerking and sticking her tongue out. When she performed “We Can’t Stop” at the
2013 V.M.A.s
, it was a brash rebuttal of her wholesome younger self. It was also a bonanza of what we might now call millennial cringe. Cyrus, who emerged onstage from inside a Teddy bear, ripped off a sparkly bodice to reveal a flesh-colored bikini. She got a little flirty with a foam finger. Robin Thicke strolled out, wearing Beetlejuice stripes, and did a verse from “
Blurred Lines
.” At one point, the camera cut to
Drake
, looking forlorn, and later to Rihanna, seated and largely expressionless. Yet “Bangerz,” which features around thirty songwriters, and production from Pharrell Williams, Dr. Luke, and Mike WiLL Made-It, remains Cyrus’s top-selling album; it débuted at No. 1 and eventually sold more than three million copies.
Cyrus has a big, blousy voice with an unmistakable country warble. Her Southernness—she was born in Franklin, Tennessee, the second daughter of the country singer Billy Ray Cyrus, and a goddaughter of
Dolly Parton
—is more palpable on her early singles, such as “Party in the U.S.A.,” a pop masterpiece from 2009. Cyrus is always more compelling when she revels in her singularity and occasional awkwardness: “My tummy’s turnin’ and I’m feelin’ kinda homesick / Too much pressure and I’m nervous,” she sings in the pre-chorus. (Who among us?) “Party in the U.S.A.” is exquisitely performed, alternately shouty and tender—even now, it’s hard to think of another singer who could have so perfectly embodied its mix of innocence and hunger.
But since “Bangerz,” Cyrus has been either casting about for an identity that feels true or embracing a postmodern disavowal of authenticity itself, depending on whom you ask. My money is on the earnest searching, though I do think that Cyrus enjoys, and excels at, character work, and has an unusual knack for inhabiting different styles. (The covers that she has done over the years, including Blondie’s “Heart of Glass” and the Cranberries’ “Zombie,” are reliably excellent.) Her penchant for reinvention feels less commercially motivated and more personal, as if she’s still trying to figure out who she really is—a process that many assume will wrap up by the close of one’s twenties (Cyrus is thirty-three) but which, in actuality, often goes on indefinitely. She followed up “Bangerz” with “
Miley Cyrus & Her Dead Petz
,” a freaky, strung-out psych-pop record that she released for free on SoundCloud. Much of the album was co-written and produced by Wayne Coyne, of the Flaming Lips, and it features tracks with blessedly stoned titles such as “Fucking Fucked Up” and “Milky Milky Milk.”
By 2017, Cyrus was covering her tattoos with makeup, wearing all white, and singing ballads of marital devotion. The
video for “Malibu,”
a single from the album “Younger Now,” shows Cyrus, then engaged to the actor Liam Hemsworth (they were married for eight months, between 2018 and 2019), on the beach, twirling in Pollyannaish ecstasy, her hair tousled by the sea breeze. She marvels at the ocean: “I never went boatin’, don’t get how they’re floatin’,” she sings, her voice full and trembly, “And sometimes I get so scared of what I can’t understand.” She released three more albums between 2020 and 2025, experimenting with indie rock and glam rock; on the single “Flowers,” the best-selling song of 2023, her sound is, by turns, folksy, retro, and disco-pop. “I can buy myself flowers,” she proclaims, “Write my name in the sand / Talk to myself for hours / Say things you don’t understand.”
I loved the confidence and ease of “Flowers”—it has the enticing swagger of Gloria Gaynor’s “I Will Survive” and Fleetwood Mac’s “Go Your Own Way,” two iconic breakup tracks. I don’t think Cyrus has ever really made an awful record. Still, received together, her albums suggest that, aesthetically, she’s something of a blank canvas. This both points toward an enviable, large-minded freedom and leaves me wondering what she actually wants to say.
Three years ago, Cyrus released “Used to Be Young,” a plaintive ballad about saying sayonara to one’s wild years. It was a bonus track on a digital reissue of “Endless Summer Vacation,” her eighth LP. The song functions as a teary-eyed encomium for a misspent youth: “You tell me time has done changed me / That’s fine, I’ve had a good run.” Cyrus was thirty when the song was released—not ancient, exactly, but not a kid, either.
Still, perhaps it was too early to light the funeral pyre. Last month, she dropped her last name (she is now known, mononymously, as Miley); on Friday, she released her tenth album, “Bass Persuades.” The title track is dark, pulsing dance pop, indebted, in obvious ways, to the trickle-down influence of
Madonna
, particularly via
Britney Spears
, Lady Gaga, and Dua Lipa. Lyrically, the song is an homage to touching grass: “Glued your eyes to the telephone screen / But you missed the hit without MTV / Go analog, make it cinema,” Miley implores. The chorus is a kind of lashing: “The kids don’t wanna dance,” she sings, over and over. Spiritually, it feels like a companion piece to Spears’s (perfect) 2003 single “Me Against the Music,” about being so moved by the beat that you have no choice but to throw ass: “I’m the only one dancin’ up in this place,” Spears sang.
Yet whereas Spears is preternaturally gifted at this sort of punchy, staccato delivery—she brings a cheerleader’s precision to her vocals, even when she is mysteriously extending the word “on” to multiple syllables—Miley’s cyclone of a voice tends to work better with looser, airier material. Dance pop favors rigor over style; each note should hit like a fist. The cadence of the title track’s spoken verses reminds me a little bit of
Charli XCX
’s “Wink Wink” and
Kesha
’s “Tik Tok,” but Miley is a belter at heart; ultimately, I found myself longing for the big-breath bombast of tunes like “Wrecking Ball” and “The Climb.”
The rest of “Bass Persuades” contains similarly sultry, twilit songs about the sort of rhapsodic, all-consuming love that makes a person go googly-eyed: “I’ve got my own God / My God’s a hot boy,” she sings on “Different Religion.” Miley is engaged to the musician Maxx Morando, who appears in the black-and-white music video for “Let’s Get Married,” one of the album’s best tracks. (In the video, the couple prance around the Chateau Marmont, partying, wearing almost nothing—and who can blame them, for they are hot.) It’s a romantic song about being so overcome by desire that you can’t wait to seal the deal: “Then he said, ‘Baby, what did I do to desеrve you? / Tell me, what did I do to dеserve you?’ / Let’s go get married tonight.” On “Orbit,” a yearning, piano-led hymn that recalls the moodiness and desperation of
Lana Del Rey
, with a hint of Heart’s “Alone,” Miley sings, “And I would bend all space and time / To fall into your hands / I’m drawn to you / I belong to you.”
“Bass Persuades” is a mix of adoring ballads and throbbing dance songs, which is not an inaccurate representation of the experience of falling for somebody—the eternal pendulum swing between lust and devotion, wantonness and hope. Yet, with the exception of “Let’s Get Married,” there isn’t a single track here that really makes me think:
Miley
. Perhaps expecting fixed self-definition from a pop star is outdated, now that our attention is irreparably fractured. Miley has always engaged with questions of persona—“Hannah Montana” is about a pop star masquerading as a regular girl, or maybe vice versa—while professing authenticity. For her, those ideas aren’t mutually exclusive. In a recent interview, she spoke about the distance between who she is onstage and who she is at her pet-filled home in L.A.: “Sometimes I call what I do drag, because the way that I present myself is just someone that is so different from the person that feeds the tortoise every morning.” She has been a professional actor, after all, for more than two decades now.
The album reminds me, in a circuitous way, of Madonna’s guest verse in “Me Against the Music”: “Sexy lady, I’d rather see you bare your soul.” It’s a quick, almost maternal rejoinder to Spears’s obsession with being seen and admired on the dance floor. “Bass Persuades” does not want for confessionalism, or vulnerability, but there is something of a personality void at its center. I would also like to see more of Miley’s soul, lest she lose track of it entirely. ♦

epub_29.title: Why America Looks the Way It Does
epub_29.text:
Why America Looks the Way It Does
A Critic at Large
Why America Looks the Way It Does
From vast grids to winding suburbs, Americans have spent two centuries remaking the landscape around property.
By Daniel Immerwahr
September 28, 2026
To Europeans, the early United States was a curiosity: rich in resources yet poor in history. They were used to a storied landscape, where it was impossible to go for a stroll without tripping over the lithic remnants of some distant era. America, by contrast, seemed blank. The French writer Alexis de Tocqueville scoffed at the “day-old ruins” of deserted log cabins—the closest thing to historical depth that this pathetically young country could manage.
He should have spent more time in Ohio. Settlers there were finding thousands of ancient Native mounds and earthworks, some bafflingly large. Refusing to believe that the ancestors of Native Americans could have built such monumental structures, writers floated bizarre theories as to who had. Perhaps it was a lost tribe of Israel, or an extinct race of giants. (Why not both?)
If oversized Jews were indeed behind it, they must have been especially fond of Pickaway County. It boasted mounds aplenty and the earthen remains of two forts, one circular and another square, constructed with startling geometric precision. In 1810, surveyors latched on to the circle and founded a city, named Circleville, in concentric arcs around it. This was “probably the only city in North America developed in a radio-concentric plan,” the historian John W. Reps wrote in 1955. (There’ve been others since.) It was also, he observed, probably the only settler city built around an Indigenous form.
Circular or not, the surveying couldn’t come soon enough. Whites were swarming into Ohio. They bought Circleville plots at a barbecue—featuring an immense, sled-drawn wheel of cheese—and raced to erect the first house. By night, several slapdash dwellings stood ready for occupancy.
It did not take long for the charms of Circleville’s bowed lots to wear off. They were hard to divvy up, and their irregular contours wasted valuable land. Rectangles would have worked better, Ohio’s government conceded. And so the Circleville Squaring Company was formed to replace Circleville’s curves with corners.
Circlevillians turned on their city like a squadron of deranged geometers. They razed the earthworks, flattened the land, rationalized property lines, and laid down straight streets. An aghast English writer warned that there would soon be “no vestige left of that peculiarity which gave the place its name, and which constituted the most perfect and therefore most interesting work of antiquity of its class in the country.” He was right; the prehistoric ruins were obliterated. Today, visitors can puzzle over a flat road called Mound Street in a square city called Circleville.
So it went in the United States. A lively new book by the historian Joshua Specht, “
Property Values
” (Princeton), considers land ownership from the country’s founding to now. It’s been two hundred and fifty years of tumult. Nineteenth-century settlers saw themselves as pioneers, breaking new ground, but, Specht notes, so did twentieth-century suburbanites. Understandably so. His book describes campaign after campaign to remake the land.
It’s often said that the original sin of the United States was slavery. Specht winces at this, not because he downplays slavery but because he regards Native dispossession as equally fundamental. The act itself was consequential, but so was the mind-set it encouraged: a tendency to treat territory as empty space. U.S. leaders stood before the map like mathematicians before a chalkboard. Circles, squares—the slate could be wiped clean as needed.
To get gravel for Circleville’s roads, workers dug into a nearby hillock. It was a burial site, they discovered, full of skeletons. They carried on. Circleville’s straightened streets were to be paved with Native bones.
It would be hard to overstate how ignorant the Founders of the United States were about their own country. The main map they’d used to negotiate the postwar peace with Britain was woefully inaccurate. It showed the Mississippi River—set as the outer border—curving adventurously west onto the Great Plains. The historian Daniel Boorstin noted that some politicians misunderstood the treaty because they’d confused the Mississippi and the Missouri. A forgivable mistake, given that they did not know where either river actually ran.
They didn’t know because those rivers wound through foreign lands. The quiet fact about the new United States was that half the territory it claimed (and far more of the continent beyond its borders) remained under Indigenous control. The largest inaccuracy of the era’s maps was to show that land as belonging to the United States.
That half-claimed Western territory might someday furnish desirable farms for settlers. Yet, even presuming that the government could beat back Native powers, intelligently dividing that unseen area into plots would require understanding its geography, soil, and waterways. Perhaps there was an easier approach, Thomas Jefferson suggested. What about drawing a gigantic grid and just partitioning the area into squares?
The grid was a familiar form, occasionally used in colonial cities, such as Philadelphia. But previous grids had been tightly bounded—patches of orthogonal civilization within an arcing and twisting terrain. What Jefferson envisaged, in contrast, was an unyielding north-south grid of continental proportions. He imagined new states as roughly rectangular, tiled end to end with square plots.
Beware straight borders on a map—they usually mean that the person drawing them knows nothing of the place in question. That was true of Jefferson, but there was an upside to his ignorance, the historian Amir Alexander argues in “
Liberty’s Grid
” (2024). The grid Jefferson proposed was neutral, agnostic, making no place more important than any other. This was connected to Jefferson’s political views, Alexander argues. In a country where all men were created equal, as Jefferson’s Declaration of Independence put it, all plots would be, too.
Congress summoned surveyors from all thirteen states to start laying down Jefferson’s grid. On September 30, 1785, surveyors from eight states got to work in what is now Ohio, just across Pennsylvania’s western border, in lands controlled by Lenapes, Miamis, Odawas, and Shawnees. After axemen cleared paths through the oaks, elms, and basswoods, the surveyors stretched a standardized measure called a Gunter’s chain—a hundred links to a chain, eighty chains to a mile—and marked the distances with tally pegs. It was a lot of fuss to make a few perforations in the earth’s surface. But those dotted lines were meant to run from the “Place of Beginning,” as the lead surveyor called it, to the distant horizon.
Jefferson’s idea was strange in many ways, but the strangest thing about it is that it took hold. By the early twentieth century, thirty-five more states had joined the original thirteen. All had at least one straight side, and several were essentially rectangles. Meanwhile, the public-land survey that began in Ohio had extended to the Pacific, covering two-thirds of the contiguous United States. As whites marched onto new lands, the grid unrolled before them like a red carpet.
Squares suited the fast-moving settlers. Certainly, they were simpler than plots defined by landmarks. Consider how one Massachusetts landowner delineated his property in that traditional system: it was “more or less bounded” by a path that started with a stake on E. Daniels’s land and then moved east “about 97 1/2 rods” to a corner of a fence, north “about 54 rods” to the corner of I. Fowler’s land, twenty-four rods toward the chestnut tree growing in the wall of Daniels’s property, and back to the stake. Compared with that morass of rustic wayfinding, where you practically had to marry Fowler’s daughter to get comprehensible directions, coördinates were bliss.
Squares made life easy for officials, too. Although the nineteenth-century state collected few taxes, it funded things with what Specht calls the “national nest egg”: its extensive landholdings. An investigation by Robert Lee and Tristan Ahtone for
High Country News
showed how this worked in higher education. To start fifty-two land-grant universities, the government used more than ten million acres it had wrested from nearly two hundred and fifty Native polities. It gave the institutions federal holdings in the West, which they could rent out or, more likely, sell. M.I.T., Cornell, Texas A. & M., Penn State, and U.C. Berkeley were among the schools launched with these grants.
The national nest egg also bankrolled the military, as soldiers could be paid partly in property. This started a vicious cycle: wars against Indians yielded land, and land funded wars. Abraham Lincoln received two parcels of federal acreage for serving less than three months in the Black Hawk War of 1832. From Illinois, where he lived, he opted for grid squares in Iowa, which he owned without ever visiting.
Eventually, the government started giving land away. The first Homestead Act, signed by Lincoln in 1862, distributed squares for free, as long as recipients went and farmed them. In a country known for its bootstrap individualism, this was a monumental handout; officials ultimately doled out an area the size of Pakistan. The vast checkerboard that airline passengers see when they fly over the West shows state socialism in action.
For settlers, gridded land came to seem natural. American football was initially played on a field of squares, hence the occasional references today to football fields as “gridirons.” Musicians use the precise markings on those fields to choreograph geometrically complex routines as part of a distinctive art form: the marching-band drill.
More consequential was the squaring of cities, like Circleville. Older settlements, such as Boston, kept their short streets and jaunty angles. But nineteenth-century ones resembled Mondrian paintings. Manhattan, straddling the two patterns, began as a typical jumble of pathways until an early-nineteenth-century planning commission imposed a grid, turning nearly everything above Fourteenth Street into a regular matrix of numbered streets intersecting numbered avenues.
The numbers are telling. In Britain and elsewhere, streets are typically named for landmarks: Station, Church, Mill, Green, and School are among the most common. In the United States, the top names are numerical—Main/First, Second, Third, and Fourth—as if its towns were coördinate planes. The numbers sometimes go disconcertingly high: to 400th Street outside Miami, 477th Avenue outside Seattle, and 571st Avenue outside Phoenix. The enumeration system starting in Roosevelt, Utah, runs ambitiously and intermittently through dozens of desert miles to reach the right-angle intersection of 6,000th South and 47,000th West.
The grid treats the Earth as if it’s flat, which, famously, it is not. Squaring off the land required property lines and related roads to perform a sort of topographical parkour, running straight over hills and across rivers. In San Francisco, the grids simply ignored the steeply sloping terrain, resulting in streets so precipitous that they make parking an extreme sport.
All this unswerving rigidity served one end: transferring property. In that, the grid succeeded marvellously. During the late nineteenth century, in what is now Oklahoma but had been Indian Territory, the government distributed some formerly Native-owned land to whoever could reach it first in a race. At the firing of a federal official’s gun, settlers scrambled to claim their squares.
Native Americans, in losing their land, lost the anchors of their worlds. Settlers, in gaining it, gained something less. Jefferson had imagined planting the countryside with farmers, but how deeply would roots grow in a property defined, as Lincoln’s was, as “N. W. ¼ of the S. W. ¼ Sec. 20 T. 84 R. 15 West in Tama Co. Iowa”? Men like Lincoln, in selecting square plots on maps, weren’t joining communities so much as amassing commodities.
Sensitive souls rebelled. Lewis Mumford, the great architectural critic, bemoaned the parcelling of land into “abstract units for buying and selling, without respect for historic uses, for topographic conditions, or for social needs.” It was pretty much a rite of passage for authors to deride Manhattan’s orthogonal streetscape: its “perpetual dead flat” (Walt Whitman), “primal topographic curse” (Henry James), or “deadly uniformity of mean ugliness” (Edith Wharton).
Nineteenth-century Romantics sought to reclaim a verdant refuge within Manhattan. This could supply “an antithesis to its bustling, paved, rectangular, walled-in streets,” the planner Frederick Law Olmsted believed. Under Olmsted’s direction, the city evicted roughly sixteen hundred New Yorkers (mostly Black or immigrant), exploded almost twenty-one thousand barrels of gunpowder, and moved more than a hundred million cubic feet of earth and stone to create Central Park. It was an Arcadia of meandering paths. Unlike the rest of Manhattan, you could get lost there.
Central Park was just the start. Olmsted also designed cemeteries, campuses, and garden-city suburbs. He even had a hand in establishing a nature preserve in the Yosemite Valley, which expanded to become today’s Yosemite National Park. It was all, Amir Alexander argues, part of a larger revolt against rectangles.
In this new light, Circleville looked different. In 1880, a local history of Pickaway County expressed regret over the obliteration of its earthworks. That relic-strewn ground, the author fumed, could have made the most “unique and attractive” park in all of Ohio.
One of the grid’s most astute late-nineteenth-century critics, the geologist John Wesley Powell, decried its environmental recklessness. Square plots might work in the East, but they’d cause ruin in the semi-arid West, he felt. Their straight lines ran roughshod across natural drainage basins, leaving some tracts unirrigated. Borders should follow water flows, not compass directions, Powell believed.
A fine idea. Yet Powell was “using bear language in a bull market,” his biographer, Wallace Stegner, wrote. The government went on gridding land, and hopeful farmers surged onto the plains, snapping up plots whose ecologies they barely understood. They enjoyed bumper crops in rainy years. But when drought struck Oklahoma and surrounding states, as drought regularly did, the topsoil dried out and blew away. Plowing up the native grasses that held that soil in place probably didn’t help.
Specht writes eloquently of the Depression-era Dust Bowl caused by an especially dire drought. The liberated dirt smothered crops and choked towns, burying farmers’ dreams in fine powder. It blew east, in great dark storms, to Boston, New York, Washington, D.C., and Atlanta. Dust rained on the White House and the Statue of Liberty.
The symbolism, for anyone who cared to notice, was rich. Whites had seized enormous swaths of unfamiliar territory. To turn it hastily into property, they’d partitioned it into squares, reducing complex geography to simple geometry. They had come for the land in droves. Now the land was coming for them.
The nineteen-thirties were a tipping point, Specht argues. If strivers in the previous decade had sought newly available farmland, their children more often sought suburban houses. The American Dream, in this sense, moved from production to consumption, from homesteaders growing crops to homeowners buying appliances. With this social shift came a spatial one, from the grid to the curve.
Again, the state blazed the trail. Whereas previously it had subsidized the mass acquisition of land, now it started subsidizing the mass purchase of houses. It did so by providing zero-down-payment loans, guaranteeing mortgages, building roads, and insuring loans to developers. The home-buying boom was “guided by government but implemented through the market,” Specht writes. This made it seem like the result of individual choices. But policies shaped those choices, and those policies strongly incentivized new, detached houses on cities’ edges. By 1960, Specht notes, “there were more Americans in suburban single-family homes than people in cities or in the countryside.”
In essence, officials helped city dwellers flee the grid. Cars made suburbs physically accessible, and subsidies made them financially so. Builders, prodded to work beyond city limits, adopted Olmsted’s vision for what those suburbs should look like. Essentially, they should look like Central Park. “Gracefully-curved lines, generous spaces, and the absence of sharp corners,” Olmsted wrote, would cultivate “contemplativeness and happy tranquillity.”
Developers sold slices of nature, but there was nothing natural about the suburbs. They were as sudden and artificial as the grids had been. The most famous postwar suburb, Levittown, on Long Island, was an explosion of 17,447 houses built in a four-year spree on failed farmland. (The farmers had daringly pursued an all-potatoes style of industrial farming only to see their tuberous cash crop ruined by an invading pest.) The builders, the Levitt family, boasted that by using assembly-line techniques they could produce a house every sixteen minutes. They’d intended to at least personalize the streets by choosing nomenclatural themes for subdivisions, but they couldn’t think of enough. Throwing in the towel, they just gave some areas street names starting with the same letter: the “D” section, the “E” section, and so on.
Throughout the nineteen-fifties, developers like the Levitts levelled an area about the size of Rhode Island every year, according to the historian Adam Rome’s “
The Bulldozer in the Countryside
” (2001). Hillocks, which interfered with mass construction, had to go. So did trees—the Levitts ripped them out to ease the work of building crews (and then planted saplings after the homes were built). It was Oklahoma all over again. Some suburbs battled soil erosion, which ruined rivers and contaminated drinking water. Others suffered dramatic landslides.
Mud and silt weren’t the only substances flowing downhill. In escaping the grid, suburbanites also escaped municipal sewer systems. Often, this meant septic tanks. These had worked adequately for isolated farmers, but too many could overwhelm the absorptive capacity of the ground—especially if sprinklers were watering the lawns—causing effluent to rise to the surface or enter waterways. In Levittown, the cost-cutting builders at first hadn’t even bothered with tanks and had installed cesspools instead—three decades later, the suburb’s sewer system was still under construction. (It could have been worse: in one Miami development, the toilets just flushed straight into front yards.) Rome describes public-health experts, having essentially vanquished raw sewage in cities, cursing the skies as it oozed through the suburbs.
Had anyone thought this through? Perhaps not, Michael Glass suggests in “
Cracked Foundations
” (University of Pennsylvania), a bracing new history of Levittown and its environs. Although curving suburbs were spatially antithetical to gridded cities, they shared one principle: speed. Most were instant communities, born of the same monomania for property sales as the grid. Glass chronicles the chaos as home buyers thronged into tracts without schools, sewers, trash removal, or viable tax bases.
The reward was homeownership. But the way to capitalize on homeownership wasn’t by sinking roots; it was by buying, building equity, and selling. This made the suburbs transient places, Glass argues. The average nineteen-fifties Levittowner left after five years.
As is well known, many suburbs were racially exclusive. The government favored loans to racially homogeneous suburban developments, and racial covenants maintained that homogeneity. In 1948, the Supreme Court found such covenants judicially unenforceable, but Specht explains how communities upheld them nonetheless. When the first Black couple moved into another Levittown, in Pennsylvania, in 1957, their neighbors burned crosses, threw stones, and gathered menacingly at their property line. The man who sold the couple that house was fired from his job.
This racial discrimination gave whites privileged access to government-backed assets—suburban houses. But, as Glass points out, condemnation of the suburbs’ racial exclusion can make it sound as if they were paradises whose only flaw was that their gates were unfairly locked. That is worth questioning.
Did
open spaces, cul-de-sacs, and “Oops, all curves” street designs make for better living?
It’s hard to say. The problem with the grid was its empty abstraction, an insensitivity to purpose that made the city a “grinding and piling up of blind forces,” in Frank Lloyd Wright’s words. Suburban developers swung hard in the opposite direction, designing large areas around specified activities. But in doing so they took the elements that had been interwoven in cities and separated them into housing tracts, office parks, industrial zones, and shopping areas. Critics compared this to eating an omelette by consuming its ingredients one by one—eggs, cheese, vegetables, oil, then salt.
Unsurprisingly, developers creating single-purpose spaces placed controls on them, and not only racial ones. Specht gives the example of Celebration, Florida, the Disney-developed suburb that opened in the nineties. Its residential area is ruled with the stringency of a Victorian governess: commercial activity is forbidden, pets and parking are restricted, and front-facing curtains must be white or—for renegades who dance on the razor’s edge of propriety—off-white. This all sounds exhausting, but most inhabitants love it, Specht notes, especially compared with the chaos of nearby Miami.
A less-noticed constraint comes from suburbia’s street layouts. Although suburban enclaves boast winding lanes, their more determining feature is their lack of intersections, the architectural theorist Albert Pope observes in his highly intelligent book “
Ladders
” (1996). Urban grids are a tight mesh of streets and junctions, meaning that any two points on them are connected by many viable routes. Suburbs, by contrast, are generally hostile to the idea of strangers barrelling through, so they have fewer streets and fewer crossings. This prevents traffic from flowing evenly, pushing it away from cul-de-sacs and go-nowhere lanes and onto a few large roads. Some communities, famously, have gates at those roads. The gatehouses prompt eye rolls, but the underlying exclusion lies in the fact that such places have so few entrances that they
can
be gated.
The unintended effect of low-density construction, restrictive zoning, and curving roads is a staggering increase in the distance between destinations. Ultimately, the cul-de-sacs designed to repel traffic increase the number of needed cars. And the more a place accommodates cars—widening main roads into smooth, unobstructed arcs—the more dangerous it becomes to walk or cycle, and the more everyone drives.
This country is now littered with developments that are called parks and gardens where it is miserable to do the one thing people like to do in parks and gardens: walk. The writer Jonathan Franzen has described a bizarre sociological phenomenon resulting from this state of affairs. Whenever Franzen, an avid urban hiker, tries his perambulations in suburban Missouri or Colorado, he sticks out so awkwardly that men in passing cars shout obscenities at him. I’ve experienced the same thing walking the winding streets of Levittown on Long Island.
The suburbs promise space yet deliver emptiness, critics charge. Even the most thoughtfully designed enclaves are suspended in a larger sprawl. For Pope, the result is a revolting phantasmagoria: the orange sodium-vapor lights of “nighttime parking lots, long abandoned agricultural fields overdraped by power lines, immaculate corporate campuses maintained in silence save for the splash of a ‘water feature,’ the brutal concrete and weeds of a freeway apron.” This is the nineteenth-century complaint about the grid—that it was soulless—applied to its opposite.
Specht adds another complaint: the suburbs have pushed politics rightward. Generally, in the United States, people get more conservative as population density falls. Even diehard Democrats seem to have felt the tug. In “
Don’t Blame Us
” (2015), the historian Lily Geismer profiles Boston’s deep-blue suburbs, full of engineers and college professors. Their inhabitants worked assiduously for integration and against war, yet they also embraced a politics of individual choice that eschewed collective spending on broader social goals. Geismer suggests that the market-forward liberalism that took hold during Bill Clinton’s Presidency can be traced to the suburbanization of the Democratic Party.
It’s tempting to see the curve as having vanquished the grid. In reality, they’re both alive, and they’re almost symbiotically bonded. Suburbs stretch their undulating freeways into the grid, sucking out nutrients (and cutting through neighborhoods). Cities, encased in suburbs, extend their ever-widening “metropolitan areas” for miles.
Specht calls for a truce between city and suburb. The government once dedicated itself energetically to distributing homesteads or homes. If such energy could go toward building up higher-density neighborhoods in lower-cost areas, a hitherto elusive “shared civic life” might be obtained, Specht suggests. It’s a sensible thought. Both the grid and the curve were simplistic, uncompromising ideas. And, when it comes to viable communities, compromise is everything.
But why did simplistic ideas hold such sway for so long? The United States has been a rootless, restless country, lunging between “Make everything squares” and “Screw squares, we’re doing circles.” Such crudely geometric thinking prevailed because the unfamiliar land seemed unmarked by history. On a stolen continent, settlers rushed onto new terrain and let their ideas run rampant. They flattened the mounds and paved the roads, bulldozing yesterday to clear space for tomorrow. ♦
