How America Became Antifascist
Franklin D. Roosevelt was slow to confront the threat of Fascism. A new history explores how he—and the country—finally came around.
By Beverly Gage
September 28, 2026
In fiction, spoiler alerts exist to protect the reader experience, premised on the idea that knowing a story’s outcome will reduce momentum and suspense. In historical writing, it’s just the opposite. Works of history gain energy from the fact that readers know where the narrative is going, especially when it’s going nowhere good. Books on the origins of wars tend to rely on a tragic arc, with the reader aware of the shoals ahead while the books’ subjects blithely reassure one another that the coast looks clear, that diplomacy will win the day, that any conflict will be short and easy.
Within this literature, no decade is more doom-laden than the nineteen-thirties, when misguided hope and willful blindness led the world’s democracies to grossly underestimate the threat of Fascism. In the standard story, the United States, Britain, and France stood by, wringing their hands and straining for appeasement while the Japanese stampeded through Asia and Nazi Storm Troopers ran roughshod over Europe. The result was the greatest cataclysm in modern history: seventy million dead, the genocide of European Jews, the bombing of once magnificent cities. The reader, aware of this outcome, is left with the literary equivalent of shouting at the screen: Don’t do it! Act now! Watch out—they’re coming for you!
The historian William I. Hitchcock’s excellent new book, “
A Shadow Over the World: Franklin D. Roosevelt, the Rise of Fascism, and the Making of America’s World War II
” (Simon & Schuster), leans into this sense of foreboding. In the course of nearly six hundred pages, Hitchcock describes how Fascism spread across the globe, beginning with Mussolini’s rise in the battered, destabilized Italy of the nineteen-twenties and ending in 1941, when Hitler occupied most of Continental Europe. A Pulitzer finalist and a professor at the University of Virginia, Hitchcock has written several books about the Second World War, each with an emphasis on the European theatre. This time, he wants to explain why U.S. policymakers, especially F.D.R., failed to act or even to fully comprehend what was happening until it was almost too late.
Unlike most coming-of-war narratives, though, “A Shadow Over the World” offers a happy ending of sorts. Hitchcock lays out a harrowing chronology of self-interested decisions, missed opportunities, and moments of cowardice as U.S. government officials debated how to meet the Fascist threat. Yet his main question is not why they failed to counter it but how, in the end, they succeeded. “In these pages,” he writes by way of introduction, “we will see an imperfect nation and an imperfect leader strive to do good after a long stretch of doing nothing in the face of fascist persecution.” What’s amazing about the era, he suggests, is not the hope, cherished by so many Americans, that war might be avoided. It’s that the nation eventually rose up and dedicated the full force of its industrial, ideological, spiritual, and military might to banishing Fascism from the earth.
To suggest that the United States in the mid-twentieth century was, at its heart, an antifascist nation is no small claim these days. In the decade-plus since Donald Trump descended his golden escalator, historians have been busy excavating what a Roosevelt aide described as the “latent Nazism” in American life. Recent books have explored Americans’ embrace of eugenics and racism, anti-egalitarianism and antisemitism, nativism and illiberal politics. They have also explored the literal Fascism that took root in the U.S. during the thirties, when avowedly pro-Nazi organizations held mass rallies at Madison Square Garden and Henry Ford cozied up to Hitler.
This work has helped make our own backlash moment more comprehensible: despite the myth of liberal progress, the reactionary and quasi-Fascist strains of American society have long been there. But the scholarly trend has obscured something that once seemed obvious—during the defining crisis of the century, the U.S. fought Fascism with everything it had. Hitchcock declares this struggle an “inspiring story of America,” with all the necessary caveats. In 1941, the aviator Charles Lindbergh may still have been praising Hitler’s air power and railing against undue Jewish influence. The federal government, though, was securely in the hands of committed antifascists. Foremost among them was Roosevelt, who maintained that democracy and Fascism could not coexist.
In Hitchcock’s telling, Roosevelt is both hero and antihero: the man who refused to heed warnings of a looming disaster—until, in the nick of time, he did. Born into a wealthy and storied political family in New York’s Hudson Valley, Roosevelt grew up expecting an easy life. For years, those expectations held firm. Though the region where he grew up leaned Republican, Roosevelt joined the Democratic Party and rose swiftly through state government. Just before the First World War, with a Democrat, Woodrow Wilson, in the White House, he was appointed Assistant Secretary of the Navy, the same post that his legendary cousin Theodore once held. In 1920, at the tender age of thirty-eight, he won a spot on the national ticket as the Party’s Vice-Presidential candidate. Although it turned out to be a Republican year, Roosevelt emerged as a rising star and a Democratic standard-bearer.
Then, in 1921, the first great tragedy of his life struck. One day in August, he came down with a fever and numbness throughout his body; by the next morning, he could not move. The culprit turned out to be polio, a dreaded disease of the pre-vaccine twentieth century. Despite the best therapies, he never regained the ability to walk unaided. Like many biographers, Hitchcock sees this physical ordeal as a turn of events that deepened Roosevelt’s character. But “A Shadow Over the World” is not primarily a biography of Roosevelt. Instead, the book offers a collective account of the “colorful, angry, tumultuous years” of his Presidency, when “chaos, fear, and profound human insecurity ruled” the globe.
For Roosevelt’s generation, no historical experience carried more weight than the First World War—or, as it was commonly known until 1939, the Great War. As Hitchcock notes, it is impossible to understand the thirties without that earlier war as a reference point: a grand cautionary tale about what to do and what not to do in response to European conflict. By the time Roosevelt became President, in 1933, most Americans viewed the war as a huge mistake. Progressives mourned the death of reform amid patriotic jingoism. Conservatives shuddered to think how close the country had come to permanent entangling alliances. Americans across the political spectrum agreed that the bloodshed had been a colossal waste of money and human life. Meant to be “the war to end war” and to make the world “safe for democracy,” it had instead produced instability, economic catastrophe, and imperial rivalry.
The war also gave new force to two powerful ideological movements, Soviet Communism and European Fascism, both of which seemed hellbent on destabilizing, then remaking, the global order. “A Shadow Over the World” is especially effective at describing the rise of Fascism in the twenties, first in Italy and then, more haltingly, in Weimar Germany. It was Benito Mussolini, not Adolf Hitler, who created the Fascist playbook: fomenting a national crisis through “political terrorism,” turning “angry young men” into thuggish enforcement agents, attacking the legitimacy of the existing government, and then demanding a new government in its place. In discussing such techniques, Hitchcock studiously avoids comparisons to the present, though one can’t help but wonder whether certain details were chosen for their current resonance. “I am in top form. Huge crowd,” Germany’s propaganda minister, Joseph Goebbels, wrote in his diary in 1933 after leading a book-burning rally.
Such moments are chilling to read about, in part because we know where they will lead. At the time, however, the meaning of Fascism wasn’t so clear. Though we now tend to view antisemitism as the ideology’s molten core, many Americans, well into the thirties, associated Fascism mainly with anti-Communism, which had its own powerful constituency. “Their chief object is to fight socialism, communism, and anarchism,” the New York
Times
wrote in an early article about Italy’s Fascisti. The Hearst newspaper chain’s first profile of Hitler made no explicit mention of antisemitism, emphasizing instead his hatred of the Bolsheviks. Even in the mid-thirties, the Chicago
Tribune
quoted one Fascist supporter in Spain explaining that “what Spaniards mean by fascist is a government that keeps order. That is what they want—that, and to destroy the Marxists.” To many Americans, early Fascism sounded less like a foreign menace than like a familiar form of anti-Communist politics.
In any case, the nation’s approach toward Europe was not to meddle in its internal affairs but, rather, to avoid another terrible Continental war. Throughout the Western world, the twenties were a period of high hopes and big thinking about global peace; the 1928 Kellogg-Briand Pact, signed by more than sixty nations, including the United States, intended to outlaw war altogether.
Once the Great Depression hit, there seemed to be even less reason to get involved in Europe’s mess. The statistics are familiar, but they bear repeating: between 1929 and 1932, the U.S. stock market lost roughly ninety per cent of its value, and unemployment reached twenty-four per cent. No wonder most Americans favored dealing with things at home rather than worrying about Europe. Some even called for a national dictator who could take the crisis in hand and get the economy functioning again. Instead, the country elected Franklin Roosevelt, who, in Hitchcock’s words, “offered them not dictatorship but democracy.”
As Hitchcock observes, Roosevelt’s personal motivations and deepest convictions are notoriously difficult to parse. As President, he often told people what they wanted to hear, not necessarily what he thought. He spent little time writing reflections or elaborating on his decision-making. Because he died in office, he left behind no retrospective summaries or grand narratives of his Presidency. His Secretary of War Henry Stimson likened conversing with Roosevelt to “chasing a vagrant beam of sunshine around a vacant room.” Historians can sympathize. Among the most persistent questions about Roosevelt is whether he possessed a coherent world view or just a topnotch set of political instincts.
Hitchcock believes that there was a there there—a few fundamental ideas and commitments that guided Roosevelt’s actions. One was the notion of interdependence, in both domestic politics and foreign affairs. “It is literally true that the ‘self-supporting’ man or woman has become as extinct as the man of the Stone Age,” Roosevelt declared, as the governor of New York. “Without the help of thousands of others, any one of us would die, naked and starved.” In Hitchcock’s account, Roosevelt eventually extended this analysis to the fight against Fascism.
It is impossible to read “A Shadow Over the World” without wondering what happened to the thoughtful, generous style of political leadership that Roosevelt embodied. Educated as a man of the world, he spoke both French and German. He devoured approximately a dozen newspapers every day, divided between morning and evening rounds. To Hitchcock, the indelible feature of Roosevelt’s Presidency was his desire to protect democratic norms and processes amid crises, even as critics accused him of being a power-mad dictator or a Communist sympathizer. “Here in America we are waging a great and successful war,” Roosevelt told the nation in 1936. “It is a war for the survival of democracy. We are fighting to save a great and precious form of government for ourselves and for the world.” Hitchcock calls those words “the thesis of the rest of his presidency.”
One question Hitchcock poses is why Roosevelt did not act sooner to confront the threat of Fascism or try to protect that “great and precious form of government” in places such as Spain, Austria, and France. Despite Hitchcock’s admiration for Roosevelt, “A Shadow Over the World” is largely an account of the President’s confusion and undue caution vis-à-vis European Fascism. The repetition can grow tiring, but that frustration is precisely the point. If Roosevelt really believed what he said, why did he wait so long to act on it?
One reason was the Neutrality Act, first passed in 1935 with Roosevelt’s reluctant support and then, in various iterations, renewed year after year, even in the wake of Italy’s invasion of Ethiopia, the Spanish Civil War, Kristallnacht_,_ and Hitler’s seizure of Austria and the Czech Sudetenland. The laws constrained the United States from selling weapons to any government actively engaged in war—an appealing idea, perhaps, but one with perverse effects. The U.S. could not sell arms to the valorous Republican government in Spain, but it was free to sell oil and grain and machinery to the Nazis (who were not, technically, at war for most of the thirties).
The laws reflected mainstream American opinion at the time: Europe’s problems were Europe’s problems. So did U.S. immigration policy, which was generally hostile to newcomers, especially Jewish ones. Despite impassioned lobbying and organizing efforts, Roosevelt kept his distance from the plight of European Jews—he was willing to express sympathy but not to open the gates. In the spring of 1939, when nearly a thousand Jewish refugees aboard the St. Louis, a German steamer, reached American waters, U.S. officials sent them back to meet their fate in Hitler’s Europe.
Even as President, Roosevelt did not single-handedly have the power to defy the Neutrality Acts or to upend the nation’s restrictive immigration laws. Still, Hitchcock wonders, couldn’t he have done more to show which side the U.S. was on? From his first moment in office, Roosevelt enjoyed overwhelming Democratic majorities in both houses of Congress. His repeated electoral victories were landslides of a sort that has become unthinkable in the twenty-first century; in 1936, he won more than sixty per cent of the popular vote and a whopping ninety-eight per cent of the Electoral College. Thanks to the New Deal, he presided over a vastly expanded administrative state that was responsive to executive direction. He also had a well-organized grassroots constituency. While Hitler was dismantling independent labor unions in Germany, Roosevelt was championing them in the U.S., which gave him a wide base of support for New Deal initiatives.
In short, Roosevelt was a strong President who showed, time and again, that he could lead the country in unlikely directions. That political power, however, came with limits. He may have had a Democratic majority, but it was a fractious one, dominated by Southern Democrats committed to preserving Jim Crow. And, as Hitchcock writes, antisemitism “coursed through the bloodstream of American public life,” including the blue-blooded foreign-policy establishment. At the White House, Roosevelt’s inner circle urged him to stay focussed on the Depression and the New Deal, the defining issues of his Presidency. Within the diplomatic corps, advisers suggested that the real global threat was the Soviet Union and the “militant left,” not whatever was happening in Italy or Germany.
Some Americans saw things differently, and their prescient warnings form the backbone of Hitchcock’s body politic. First among them is the newspaper columnist Dorothy Thompson, who secured an interview with Hitler in 1931 and spent the rest of the decade sounding the alarm about what she described as the Nazis’ “peculiar mixture of Nordic myth, antisemitism, militaristic tradition, desperado nationalism and moronized socialism.” Thompson was widely celebrated in her day as the “First Lady of American Journalism.” (She was also the wife of the novelist Sinclair Lewis, whose book “
It Can’t Happen Here
” stoked worries about homegrown Fascism.) As Hitchcock puts it, she was “almost Roosevelt’s alter ego,” the Cassandra who saw what was coming when the President couldn’t, or wouldn’t.
Thompson had her share of allies. “A Shadow Over the World” brings to life the vibrant antifascist “network” around Roosevelt, filled with journalists and policymakers and civic leaders desperate to make the White House listen. Their ranks included luminaries such as Ernest Hemingway, the Interior Secretary Harold L. Ickes (“the most outspoken antifascist in the cabinet”), and the rabbi Stephen Wise, all of whom deployed their public influence to spread the word about Nazi atrocities. Hitchcock also gives due credit to the many women at the forefront of that same effort, including the Labor Secretary Frances Perkins, the reporter Martha Gellhorn (who later married Hemingway), and the First Lady, Eleanor Roosevelt. On this issue, as on so many others, Eleanor was out ahead of her husband.
Hitchcock’s point in mapping this network is not just to provide a contrast to Roosevelt. He argues that the antifascist opinions and strategies developed in such circles provided a framework for national opinion and policy once events drew the U.S. into war. Given Hitchcock’s interest in this broader civic context, it is surprising that he does not pay more attention to the Popular Front, the uneasy coalition of Communists, socialists, liberals, and progressives that defined left-wing politics in the late thirties. Though Popular Front groups took on domestic issues such as labor and civil rights, antifascism was their raison d’être. Indeed, it was the Stalin-dominated Comintern that called for such a coalition in 1935 to oppose the urgent threat of global Fascism. Years later, during the Red Scare, American Communists joked that their greatest crime was to have been “prematurely antifascist” in an age when few Americans were prepared to face reality.
Although the antifascist left may have been vindicated by history, the widespread association of antifascism with Communism helps explain why Americans, including Roosevelt, came so late to the cause. During the thirties, anti-Communism was at least as powerful as antifascism in the U.S., and many Americans expressed skepticism about any political movement associated with Moscow. In 1938, when the Texas congressman Martin Dies, Jr., became chairman of a House committee tasked with investigating “un-American activities,” his putative aim was to go after Communists and Fascists equally. The Communist Party did itself no favors the following year when, in the wake of the Nazi-Soviet non-aggression pact, it performed an about-face on Fascism. The pact was a disaster for the Popular Front, but the severing of the ideational link between Communism and antifascism probably helped the antifascist cause at home. After 1939, it became possible—and necessary—to envision an antifascist politics that could be defined as truly American.
According to Hitchcock, Roosevelt always “instinctively hated fascism.” But not until 1939 did he start to embrace the idea that a literal war against actually existing Fascist powers would be both desirable and inevitable. The title “A Shadow Over the World” comes from a speech Roosevelt delivered that September, just weeks after Hitler invaded Poland, launching the Second World War. “I should like to be able to offer the hope that the shadow over the world might swiftly pass,” he told Congress. “I cannot. The facts compel my stating, with candor, that darker periods may lie ahead.”
At last, he sounded more like Dorothy Thompson, unflinching and resolute. Even so, it would take more than two years for the U.S. to enter the war. Hitchcock thinks that putting the right ideas in place was a necessary first step; without Roosevelt’s early articulation of aims, it would have been impossible to mobilize American society on the epic scale required for total war. Over the past half century, Americans have grown accustomed to regional conflicts fought by specialized professional troops, in which the support of Congress or the American public seems more or less irrelevant. The Second World War demanded mass buy-in; every factory, every worker, every young man, every housewife had to play a role. Hitchcock maintains that persuasion had to come first—that, for a democracy to fight, its citizens must know what they are fighting for. “The Second World War was at its heart a war of ideas,” he concludes.
But ideas go only so far. If the Second World War was an ideological war, it was also an economic and bureaucratic one, fought for control of the world’s raw materials and industrial capacity. When it came to the practicalities of mobilization, administrative competence proved at least as important as high-flown rhetoric. So did the capability to manufacture vast quantities of airplanes, tanks, and bullets. Hitchcock believes that Roosevelt’s New Deal vision blended seamlessly with his war aims; both emphasized democracy, collective action, and global interdependence. New Deal experiments also helped build the bureaucratic infrastructure that made the war effort possible.
In the end, it was neither ideas nor organization—neither Thompson nor Roosevelt—that persuaded the U.S. to enter the war. The Japanese did that, when they attacked Pearl Harbor, in December, 1941. As a historian of the European theatre, Hitchcock devotes only a single chapter to Japan’s imperial expansion in Asia during the thirties. He also ends his book before Pearl Harbor, arguing that the essential features of the American war effort, including the national commitment to fighting Fascism, were in place by then. For Hitchcock, the turning points came earlier, in 1940 and 1941, as Hitler blitzed his way through Continental Europe. Moved more by geopolitical reality than by idealism, Roosevelt began to insist that the U.S. would have to aid Britain—and fight Fascism—or face the extinction of democracy.
By the fall of 1941, much of the country had come to agree with him, though influential groups, such as the isolationist America First Committee, mounted fierce opposition. Hitchcock highlights key moments of escalating national commitment: Roosevelt’s “Four Freedoms” speech, on January 6, 1941, with its rousing statement of war aims; the creation of the lend-lease policy that March, with its promise of virtually unlimited arms for Great Britain; and the release of the Atlantic Charter, in August, 1941, jointly issued by Roosevelt and Winston Churchill, which envisioned a postwar order characterized by free trade, democratic rights, economic security, and territorial stability. The implication is that the U.S. would have entered the war and fought the good fight even without Pearl Harbor. But it’s worth remembering that the U.S. did not declare war on Germany until December 11th, four days after the Japanese attack. Even then, Hitler was the first mover. Only after Germany declared war on the U.S. did the U.S. respond in kind.
After the war ended, of course, anti-Communism became the guiding principle in U.S. foreign policy, bringing Washington into friendly relations with Franco’s Spain, Salazar’s Portugal, and military dictatorships elsewhere. But antifascism remained a vital part of Americans’ self-conception, as if entering the war and winning it had always been America’s destiny. Hitchcock’s book restores a sense of contingency to that story, even as it tries to draw lessons from the nineteen-thirties. One might conclude from America’s halting embrace of antifascism during that decade that we should listen to the Dorothy Thompsons of the world, who warn that the unthinkable—global war, societal collapse, genocide—really can happen. The difficulty is knowing which Dorothy Thompsons to listen to. False certainty is common enough in political life, and history is crowded with confident warnings that proved wrong. Roosevelt is arguably the more useful example, precisely because of his hesitation, pragmatism, and self-interest. What made him a great President, in Hitchcock’s view, was his willingness to watch and listen, and to change his mind as events unfolded.
“A Shadow Over the World” describes Roosevelt’s “evolution from an anti-war pacifist, a nationalist, and an American exceptionalist to a man who embraced a stunningly ambitious global task: the safeguarding of democracy in a world that had fallen under the shadow of fascism.” But Roosevelt did not abandon American exceptionalism, even as he made his case for global war. Instead, he sought to transform what it meant—not the land grabs of Manifest Destiny or the imagined security of isolationism but a commitment to defending democratic ideals and basic human welfare in the face of global tyranny and immiseration.
Roosevelt’s blind spots and foot-dragging are worth remembering as a counterpoint to the self-congratulatory Greatest Generation myth. But, as Hitchcock notes, the remarkable thing is that he changed his mind at all, and that the nation followed. For the rest of the twentieth century, America’s role in combatting Fascism helped define its national identity. At a moment when that self-conception seems to be waning, “A Shadow Over the World” makes a vigorous case for antifascism as a central inheritance of the modern American political tradition. ♦

Briefly Noted
Books
Briefly Noted
“The Radiance,” “Cloudthief,” “Dear Dealer,” and “Citizen Beast.”
September 28, 2026
The Radiance
, by Ayad Akhtar (Summit)
. The narrator of this form-bending novel is a man who shares the author’s name and profession, and who, at the story’s outset, is the victim of a hit-and-run. When he wakes up in a hospital, he finds himself transformed with new insight: “I suddenly felt I was seeing not with my eyes, but through my chest.” To his dismay, he realizes that “language is insufficient to the task” of imparting his experience, and as he struggles to make sense of this change—or perhaps because of it—he is increasingly attuned to the darkness plaguing friends and strangers alike. “I was baffled that words had ever been able to distract me from my disgust at the gratuitous welter beyond them,” Ayad remarks, prompting readers to reflect on their own insulation.
Cloudthief
, by Nathaniel Rich (MCD)
. This hardboiled heist story follows a pair of down-and-out lovers from Manhattan to Oklahoma as they attempt to steal hard drives from a towering data center. Tim, an impressionable and unscrupulous journalist, is pulled into the scheme by the wily Virginia, a decrepit but beautiful woman he meets while attempting to rob the storage unit she lives in. Their idea—to leverage sensitive personal and business information contained in the servers for an enormous ransom—is both ridiculous and ingenious. Although the novel’s meditations on technology and the environment can be tedious, the time it spends tracking these two on their adventure (which makes up the majority of the book) is brisk and entertaining.
What We’re Reading
Discover notable new fiction, nonfiction, and poetry.
Dear Dealer
, by Nadia Bowers (Gallery)
. Expanded from a piece for “This American Life,” this memoir charts the aftermath of the death, from an opioid overdose, of the author’s sister, Sasha. Written as a series of letters to Sasha’s unknown dealer, Bowers’s book offers her a way to process her grief and parse her relationship with her sister. Sasha’s addiction began from attempts to suppress Tourette’s tics: she took over-the-counter sedatives first, before turning to synthetic opioids. Bowers recounts repeatedly examining Sasha’s cellphone in the hope of identifying the person who sold her deadly drugs—a quest that she ultimately acknowledges is futile. “I’ve been using you. Like a fix,” she admits to the phantom dealer. “It’s hard to imagine my life without you. But I need to try.”
Citizen Beast
, by Martin Devecka (Johns Hopkins)
. Drawing on a variety of sources—from philosophical treatises to poems and popular jokes—this compact study shows how writers of the Roman era rendered animals, domestic and wild, as imperial subjects. Whether kneeling supplicants (elephants), gladiatorial executioners (bears), agricultural laborers (oxen), or divine messengers (birds), animals were imagined as active (which is not to say free) participants in the creation and expansion of the Empire, with roles that complemented those of their human counterparts, élites as well as enslaved people. While unearthing these depictions, Devecka argues that they formed “part of a social project that aims to degrade and subjugate human beings and other animals alike.”

epub_32.title: Gut Renos of Ionesco and Chekhov

Gut Renos of Ionesco and Chekhov
The Theatre
Gut Renos of Ionesco and Chekhov
In “Delirium” and “The Cherry Orchard,” experimental directors smash up and rebuild classic plays.
By Emily Nussbaum
September 24, 2026
Igor Golyak’s “Delirium,” a madcap, sneakily emotional reinvention of the 1962 Eugène Ionesco play “Frenzy for Two, or More,” opens with an alarming tableau: a dust-coated man is lying face down, crushed by a heavy door that covers his back like a turtle’s shell. He wears an infantry helmet but also a fancy suit with a cummerbund, and after wriggling out from under the door he props it up so that it faces him, knocks on it in a panic, and finally “breaks in” to the room he’s created. Then, making himself at home, he sits on a stack of four mattresses, which emit a loud groan. The night I attended, the audience giggled uneasily—a woman was clearly trapped down there, pancaked between mattresses as if buried in rubble. The man rescued her, but first he bounced on the bed a bit, experimentally, playing her groans like a piano.
This is our introduction to He and She, two clownish, pugilistic lovers who are locked in a war of words, even as a literal war rages outside. Golyak, an avant-garde director trained in Moscow, has made a set of aggressive edits to Ionesco’s surreal post-Second World War farce, trimming roles, amping up the slapstick, and framing the stage in industrial scaffolding draped with wobbly sheets of corrugated metal, which threaten to come crashing down. Golyak has added a big orange fish, which floats buoyantly in an aquarium, and he’s replaced the tatty bathrobes that Ionesco gave the couple with seedy Vegas finery, as if they’d dressed for a party that will never start. He’s made elegant additions, too, such as stitching in a lovely fairy tale that Ionesco wrote for his daughter and staging it with a whimsical storm of soap bubbles. Still, the core of the show remains the same: a couple ignores a public battle for a private one. Early in the play, She fumes at He, “A snail and a turtle, they’re the
same thing!
” Later, He holds up a telephone and insists it’s cheese. When grenades fly through their windows, they toss them back out, eager to resume their debate.
Golyak, whose parents fled Ukraine for Boston when he was nine, is the scrappy founder of Arlekin, a theatre company in Needham, Massachusetts, that is composed mainly of immigrants. His inventive productions often explore real-life stories of violence and displacement, including the much praised “Our Class,” which centers on an infamous pogrom in which Poles burned their Jewish neighbors to death in a barn. “Delirium,” in contrast, feels universal, a serum synthesized after the Second World War that still applies to modern wounds. He and She could be stuck in any war, in any room, anywhere in the world. And yet their repartee, full of insults (“Seducer!”) and loony demands (“Give me the definition of ‘insinuation’!”), is warped in the way contemporary language is warped: they’re gaslighting and trolling each other, like posters on some ancient Reddit thread that can no longer be parsed by outsiders. On the director’s Substack, “Theater of Questions,” he describes Ionesco’s absurdist scenario as a “shell” emptied of meaning, and this is true on multiple levels: the words are placeholders shuffled around in a deceptive game; they suggest scattered bullet casings, the residue of violence; they are safe places to hide out in, a rigid cover for vulnerable beings—turtles, snails, refugees—who are looking for comfort. But Golyak’s most significant intervention is to amplify the central romance, by slicing in flashes of sensuality and warmth, making He and She seem less like nemeses than like intimate partners, constructing a bridge of private jokes that allows them to shimmy their way past dread.
“Delirium” also felt like a relief to me—it offered a break from the usual polemic realism. Absurdity can be a liberation: it’s permission to stop making sense, an open door to ambiguity. Still, what makes Golyak’s production really roar into flame is the astonishing magnetism of his performers, Chulpan Khamatova, a Russian theatre and movie star who fled her homeland because of Putin’s invasion of Ukraine, and Andrey Burkovskiy, a celebrated Russian figure skater and actor. They’ve got Chaplin chops, with Khamatova a mischievous Kewpie doll in a mop-top blond wig and Burkovskiy a craggy acrobat whose expressions shift, like tectonic plates, from petulance to yearning. In Golyak’s vision, these two are not dead-eyed Rock ’Em Sock ’Em robots but flawed, tender humans who are vain, silly, angry, defensive, horny, innocent, and triumphant. Mainly, however, they’re terrified, and determined to fend off that fear. They eavesdrop on their neighbors, who are being kidnapped or, perhaps, tortured. Objects tumble from the scaffolding; bombs explode. But the couple’s focus is ultimately on each other. When a bullet flies into the room, each instinctively turns and asks, “Are you hurt?” Only once they know that they’re safe can the game begin again.
Simon Stone’s glamorous renovation of Chekhov’s tragicomic masterpiece “The Cherry Orchard” attempts something similar, with less success. In Stone’s version of the play, which is performed in Korean with English subtitles, he retains Chekhov’s plot about a fading aristocratic clan in denial about the sale of its home, but he dilutes the poetry, simplifies the characters, and flattens the themes, producing something like a deep-plane facelift—it’s pretty but unnervingly smooth. Stone’s “Cherry Orchard,” set in modern Seoul, is about a spoiled, wealthy family, the Songs, who run a corporation that is on the verge of collapse, owing to the family’s mismanagement. In place of a decrepit manor, the Songs live in a fabulous modernist mansion with a high-peaked slanted roof that cascades, in dramatic fashion, all the way to the ground in the form of a wide, tiered staircase, calling to mind a game of Chutes and Ladders—some characters will rise, others will tumble down. The actors regularly jog up to the peak, where they declaim their political beliefs, brood, or threaten suicide. The front of the house is all glass—a lousy place to throw stones.
That set, which was designed by Saul Kim, is genuinely spectacular to look at, as are the bright, casual costumes and the clever lighting. The cast is game, too, particularly Son Sang-kyu, who is very funny as a feckless chatterbox with a thing for retro record players, and Moon Choi, who plays the moodier, more legitimately aggrieved of two Song daughters. I was initially intrigued by Stone’s commitment to laughs, with the “tragi-” ripped off Chekhov’s comedy like a sales tag. Unfortunately, the results, while splashily entertaining, feel helium-light instead of morally weighty, with each encounter at once high-stakes and emotionally obvious. The players flatly declare their judgments: “She has ideas well above her station. It’s not appropriate.” They get sloppy drunk, then trauma-dump or make ill-advised passes, then apologize. By the final act, Chekhov’s subtle, empathetic, often unspoken power dynamics feel transmuted into a soapy romp that gestures at the class-warfare themes of “Succession” or “Parasite,” but without the former’s black wit or the latter’s pungency.
Instead, there’s a Bravo oomph to the shenanigans. Jeon Do-yeon, who plays the family’s matriarch, is colorfully slinky as a globe-trotting party widow, a vain, compulsively seductive narcissist who macks on her daughters’ men like a Real Housewife given a villain’s edit. A set of interlocking love triangles scores harsh laughs off familiar archetypes: a fuckboy, an incel, a soy boy, a finance bro who won’t commit. But farce can take you only so far. When there are glimmers, here and there, of unexpected angles—a sweet, strange speech about an abandoned turntable; the gentle bond between the younger Song daughter and a left-wing scholar—they quickly dissolve, subsumed by the archly satirical twists of the plot. Without authentic longing, and without any bittersweet complexity to the portrait of one social order replacing another, we’re left with little more than puffs of amusement, enough to escalate your mood but bound to fade by morning. ♦

The Predator Catcher Turns Predatory in “Primetime”
The Current Cinema
The Predator Catcher Turns Predatory in “Primetime”
A dazzling, wolfish performance from Robert Pattinson anchors Lance Oppenheim’s period piece about the rise and fall of a reality-TV host.
By Justin Chang
September 25, 2026
The title of “Primetime,” Lance Oppenheim’s thriller about the making and unmaking of the scuzzy reality-TV phenomenon “To Catch a Predator,” tells us we’re watching a period piece. The period is 2006, when the golden age of streamable content is barely a speck on the media horizon. YouTube is less than a year old, Netflix is a DVD-by-mail service, and a prime-time slot is still one of the most coveted jewels in broadcast television. Of the many throwback jolts that “Primetime” aims to deliver, none is more jarringly analog than the sight of a TV schedule on a wall at NBCUniversal’s offices, with shows like “Gilmore Girls” and “Veronica Mars” stacked on primary-colored planks. When the network’s C.E.O., Jeff Zucker—played, in a vertiginous mix of authenticity and uncanny-valley weirdness, by Zucker himself—announces that he’s moving “To Catch a Predator” to Wednesdays at 9
P
.
M
., he actually
moves
it, with his hand. Spreadsheets existed in 2006, but here they are kept, like everyone’s shame and scruples, firmly out of sight.
With “To Catch a Predator,” Chris Hansen (Robert Pattinson), the show’s immaculately suited host, and Andie Bender (Merritt Wever), his formidable producer, have transformed a popular segment on the news magazine “Dateline NBC” into a skin-crawling sensation. The opening scenes of “Primetime,” which was written by Ajon Singh, set up the format of the show, which is itself an elaborate setup—a trap laid for men soliciting sex with minors. One such mark (Tony Revolori) turns up at a suburban address, expecting to find a thirteen-year-old girl he’s met online. Little does he know that the house is rigged with cameras, and that a TV crew supervised by Bender is hiding inside. He’s welcomed in by a “decoy” (Phoebe Bridgers), an adult passing for a minor, and then the trap is sprung: Hansen emerges and confronts the man with a smirk, a damning transcript of illicit chat messages, and the news that all this is being recorded for television. After some squirmy interrogation, the disgraced target is asked to leave—at which point he’s arrested outside by armed police officers, who have been working closely with the crew.
It’s a queasily compelling spectacle, though perhaps also a redundant one. Even for those of us who didn’t watch “To Catch a Predator” when it aired, from 2004 to 2007, the documentary “Predators,” which was released last year, told us more than we could have ever wanted to know. Its director, David Osit, sifting through hours of “Catch” footage and interviewing its original participants, asked tough questions about the ethics of an enterprise that presented itself as a moral crusade but was ultimately torn apart by competing imperatives: Was this a law-enforcement tool, a piece of entertainment, or both? “Predators” was thoughtful and productively disturbing, at least until its posturing final moments, when Osit, interrogating a proudly unrepentant Hansen, tried to turn the show’s formal devices against him: split-screen surveillance footage, a post-interview walk of shame. It was a clever but hollow bit of visual mimicry, a halfhearted takedown that devolved into a futile shrug.
“Primetime,” as it happens, is Oppenheim’s first stab at fiction. He previously directed the documentary features “Some Kind of Heaven” (2021), a panoramic portrait of a retirement community, and “Spermworld” (2024), which explored the growing online market for sperm donations—the end and the beginning of life in two wittily framed, dryly observant films. Both were shot by David Bolen, whom Oppenheim has retained for “Primetime.” Their work here evokes the grubby, pixellated textures and the seedy-dreamy ambience of a bygone trash-TV era. The atmosphere persists even when the characters are off the air, as if to suggest that the seeping rot of the show has metastasized into every moment of their lives. The frame is squarish in shape, recalling the years before wide-screens were widespread; the colors, especially the flesh tones, are luridly oversaturated. At times, Oppenheim zooms in on his characters so intently that he seems ready to claw their faces off, the better to penetrate through to their darkest depths.
But what would he find? Pattinson’s dazzlingly contoured performance doesn’t provide any easy answers. His Chris Hansen is all flashy surface, full of jittery go-getter energy and disturbingly devoid of inner life. At NBC, he’s a second-tier golden boy, stuck in the shadow of the “Dateline” anchor Stone Phillips (Bill Heck), who’s off doing serious reporting in places like Afghanistan. (The war on terror, the film suggests, was one of the few things that could command American attention spans in the early two-thousands, along with Britney Spears and reality TV.) Meanwhile, Hansen’s work has taken a toll on his family life in Stamford, Connecticut, where he occasionally drops in on his wife (Anna Faris) and their two young sons. Then it’s back on the road to sniff out sex offenders in towns like Fort Myers, Florida, where one of Hansen’s extramarital affairs has attracted the notice of the
National Enquirer
. The irony of America’s most famous entrapment artist facing his own public humiliation is not lost on him.
Challenged on all sides, Hansen finds that his only recourse is to throw himself, with ever more frenzied self-seriousness, into his work. Sitting down with Dan Plum (Skyler Gisondo), a naïve yet ambitious twenty-three-year-old who’s been cast as a decoy, Hansen denies that what they’re doing has any relation to acting; they’re in the truthtelling business. His own behavior belies that notion. Preparing to make his “gotcha!” entrance, Hansen rehearses the incriminating chat messages that he plans to read: “I will undress you, and you will undress me,” he murmurs, and Pattinson, magnificently repellent, draws out the juicy salaciousness in every word. If you saw the actor’s dual performances in “Mickey 17” (2025), you know that his single most chameleonic attribute is his voice, which he can inflect and distort with virtuosic skill. No less slippery are his matinée-idol looks, which can turn wolfish or ratty on a dime, as if his beauty were moldering away from within. Again and again, Pattinson evinces a pig-in-shit delight in his characters’ rough edges, frayed nerves, and devious motives—not that Hansen would ever admit to the last, convinced as he is of the nobility of his cause. “We are cleansing the world of an ancient evil,” he declares.
His colleagues are not so high-minded, and as pressures and budgets mount—more episodes, fresh locations, higher-profile targets—the film becomes a vision of something strikingly relatable: the low-morale workplace. When Bender considers moving to a rival network, Wever fleshes out the tough carapace of a woman who, even under the thorniest of circumstances, never stops calculating her next move. “Decoy Dan,” as Hansen christens him, just wants to be an actor, and Gisondo shows the layers of the young man’s confusion, vulnerability, and desperation as he realizes how limited his opportunities are. The team’s creepiest and most contented member is Xavier Von Erck (Matthew Maher), an online vigilante who arranges the show’s meetups, spending his days and nights fishing around in online chat rooms.
And what of the fish? Like “Predators,” “Primetime” allows us to feel a twinge of pity on their behalf. One target has a disability; another turns out to be a rabbi, who responds to his confrontation with suitably Talmudic indignation. Singh’s script climaxes with the fatal 2006 incident that ultimately took “To Catch a Predator” off the air—a would-be predator’s suicide, triggered by the zealous overreach of the show’s camera crew and the police. But the film’s depiction of the tragedy feels cynical and rote, and one shot in particular, all meticulously art-directed blood spatter, throws the aesthetic virtues and dramatic limitations of “Primetime” into sharp relief. Oppenheim has persuasively rendered a grotesque phenomenon, but his curiosity seems to stop at how everyone and everything looked. There’s no deeper analytical heft to the movie, no larger curiosity about what “To Catch a Predator” meant then or what it might mean now, especially in the wake of the sex-trafficking conspiracy theories of QAnon and the very real, still emerging horrors of the Epstein files.
Hansen, who left NBC in 2013 but remains a leader in the pervert-ambushing space, has spoken about having considered a sting operation against Jeffrey Epstein in 2015. The men he exposed are small-timers by comparison, although Oppenheim has cast them with a nasty, stunt-like relish, starting with Revolori, who came to fame as a fresh-faced young bellhop in “The Grand Budapest Hotel” (2014). Another offender is played by Jonathan Lipnicki, whom some will remember as the cherubic kid from “Jerry Maguire” (1996), and who here has graduated to doing unspeakable things with whipped cream. The most tortured of the lot comes to us in the form of Alex Winter, now all but unrecognizable as the youthful co-lead of “Bill & Ted’s Excellent Adventure” (1989). By the time you
do
recognize him, you may let out a grim chuckle at what I can only assume is Oppenheim’s expression of sympathy for the Devil—a reminder, if we needed it, that every child predator was once a child, too. ♦

epub_35.text:
Weeping Willow, Nantucket
Poems
Weeping Willow, Nantucket
By Stephanie Burt
September 27, 2026
They can’t get off the island either.
That’s why their resolve to bend and never break—
itself about to break
when the worst winds come—
gives them their only course; their versets turn inward,
like artichoke prickles, and overlap, almost awkward,
a way to repel, and accept, the pelting weather.
That’s how it feels in the rain. They hold together.
In sun, the willow shakes their loosened limbs, then sweeps them out
to take in the neediest seekers, looking out
for cottontails, squirrels, killdeer, and the lovers who come
for privacy and don’t seem to mind
how dirty their cutoffs’ butts get. They’re of one mind.
Some catkins dangle low enough to feather
a forehead, or tickle and bother
some friends-to-lovers arc, or scratch
the lawn where nosy seagulls start from scratch.
Sometimes the willow thinks one of their neighbors has come
to look down on them: the beach rose
swinging her hips, or the high oak that throws
its own shade, or else the spray of blooming heather
on the hill. But only the willow means shelter.
Only the willow offers so many fine arrows,
directions for the patience that arose
in us when we first found these canopies’ welcome,
their design (a design for living: pale, supple) that grows
from the willow’s fingertips, those jointed rows
that draw, and withdraw, and revive. They could live here forever.
This is drawn from “Read the Room.”

epub_36.title: D’Angelo in Starlight
epub_36.text:
D’Angelo in Starlight
Poems
D’Angelo in Starlight
By Ishion Hutchinson
September 27, 2026
Good God, the devil is up to his old tricks.
His old jealous awe, being where it should not.
He rides aslant blue ether. He brings down that
voice of reed and steel. He whistles like a
comet through a crooked tooth sweat a chain
gang’s moan. The brightest falls when he whistles.
As it falls, brightens the Archer’s black hole.
Stars grow quiet mid-sea. Goddammit, he
skins the brightest he mirrors, cuts clean strings
of wind, the bastard of history repeats
all that iron deposit of bad rain.
He can swell a man’s lunar hours big
with a haunt no root-work spell could undo.
Not a preacher’s lash, not the devil’s tongue.
He is both and none. Waiting at the gate.

Letters from Our Readers
The Mail
Letters from Our Readers
Readers respond to M. R. O’Connor’s story about smokejumpers, Kelefa Sanneh’s piece about A.I. music, Jennifer Wilson’s article about lingerie, and Anna Holmes’s home-ownership essay.
September 28, 2026
Things of Nature
I was intrigued by M. R. O’Connor’s article about wildland firefighters who leap out of airplanes (“Going Up in Smoke,” September 7th). My father was a smokejumper from 1948 to 50, flying out of a base in Idaho City. He certainly had the “it” that O’Connor captures—that remarkable combination of fortitude, discipline, and high risk tolerance. These qualities served him well. He worked his way into the professional class by joining the U.S. Air Force and then using the G.I. Bill to attend dental school. It was only when I read O’Connor’s piece that it occurred to me that his training as a smokejumper was what enabled him to survive being shot down over Korea, and then to endure being a prisoner of war.
Unfortunately, the horrors of that experience never released him. For the rest of his life, he was plagued by night terrors. The only time I saw him at peace was when he was in the backcountry wilderness. The suggestion of creating a “modern G.I. Bill” for those who work on fire and trail crews is a good one. I wonder what my father’s life would have been like if, as a society, we rewarded the care and preservation of our natural environment, rather than violence and destruction in other lands.
Kathleen M. Pape, Psy.D.
Seattle, Wash.
Something Borrowed
While I appreciated Kelefa Sanneh’s analysis of how A.I. is used to compose music, I noticed that he overlooked how human composers, myself included, learn and create (Pop Music, September 7th). Composers of both classical and popular music study what came before them, absorbing and reworking earlier melodies, harmonies, rhythms, and techniques. Beethoven urged musicians to study Handel and learn “how to achieve great effects, by such simple means,” and Stravinsky is quoted as saying, “A good composer does not imitate; he steals.” In the realm of popular music, Paul McCartney admitted, “For me, the first thing was to copy other people, like Buddy Holly and Little Richard—and Elvis.”
Similarly, A.I. analyzes existing music and generates new combinations from what it has gleaned. Though that raises legitimate questions about copyright, consent, and compensation, learning from earlier music is hardly an invention of A.I. Indeed, completely original music, unconnected to anything a listener has previously heard, would perhaps be impossible to understand. Originality often lies not in creating from nothing but in transforming what already exists.
Jason Eyster
Chelsea, Mich.
Femme Fatale
Jennifer Wilson, in her piece on lingerie, gathers the evidence for an argument she doesn’t quite make (“Strange Bedfellows,” September 14th). The right hasn’t simply taken sexy back; it has redefined who gets to be sexy and drawn a hard line around “real” women. Take the American Eagle Outfitters ad that Wilson describes, with its genetic determinism and praise for Sydney Sweeney’s “great jeans.” Wilson reads the ad as a joke about Sweeney’s “supposed physical supremacy” that seemed to give “free press to a right-wing talking point.” But the ad, by presenting Sweeney’s body as proof of heritable womanhood, served conservatives in another way, too. A “real” woman in their narrative is a cisgender, fertile one; trans women and nonbinary people have no place. Lingerie-clad conservatives and liberals now may look strikingly alike—but on the right only some women get to be sexy. It isn’t just a fashion trend. It’s a boundary intended to keep people out.
Leora Tanenbaum
New York City
Home Truth
I’d like to offer a perspective different from Anna Holmes’s on the difficulties of homeownership (The Weekend Essay, September 12th, newyorker.com/holmes-on-homeownership). Holmes is surrounded by friends who are rich. This is the case for a lot of people who, like myself, live in New York and work in media. Here’s the thing I’ve learned: though there are some people with generational wealth and good financial habits, none of them are twenty-five. If you’re of a lower socioeconomic status and have mainly wealthy friends, you’ll probably pick up all of their bad habits and none of the good ones necessary to buy a home.
My husband and I purchased a three-bedroom, three-bathroom house in South Slope, Brooklyn, without the help of generational wealth. We did it by saving and by investing. During our twenties, it took tremendous effort to avoid the behavior of our wealthy friends, who would go to every wedding, spend their entire paychecks, and enroll in graduate school without a second thought. Such decisions will cause the kind of frustration Holmes describes. But I’m not making a who-made-better-choices argument—I wanted to go on the European castle trips I was invited to, too. It’s just that it is hard to make good decisions in a society that values all of these things.
I was financially literate, which gave my husband and me a head start, but friendships are what ultimately made the difference. We enrolled our son in a local public school and surrounded ourselves with people who had the financial habits we had to normalize in order to eventually own property. These kinds of friends have advice, and they will help you. Spend your time with them, not the ones who will grumble about a vacation home you’ll never have.
Bourree Lam
Brooklyn, N.Y.
